  • A project permission given for the whole organization counts in every project; given on a project, in the project (and its sub-projects when the row says so).
  • The rows for the whole organization, and a role's own field and people levels, are changed only with Decide who has which role or Decide what roles see from a row for the whole organization.
  • Moving a project takes Move projects at the old and at the new parent; a project at the top level counts as inside the organization, so moving to or from the top takes the permission for the whole organization. Making a top-level project takes Make projects; a sub-project takes Make sub-projects at its parent. Renaming a project takes Change project settings; changing its short name takes that and also the right to make projects where the project sits (Make projects at the top level, Make sub-projects at the parent), because a short name that is taken is told only to people who may make projects there (owner decision of 2026-10-06: keep). A move shows its preview first (who gains or loses access or changes role, which fields and kinds of people information change for whom: the difference of two evaluations, bb_policy::preview_move) and is refused when somebody could take away a No access that applies to them after it and could not before (ADR-0025, decision 6; M2-F23). Changing a project's short name takes Change project settings and the right to make projects where the project sits, because only those people may be told that a short name is taken.
  • Later milestones add their permissions to the enum (issues M3, time M6, documents M11), each with its topic, sentence, kind and starting values. Enforced by: ARCH-PERMS (a permission without a route or a message fails).

Assignments

An assignment is one row of Who has which role:

PartValues
Whoa person, or a group
Whata role, or No access
Where it countsWhole organization (rows in Organization settings), Only this project, This project and its sub-projects (rows on a project); No access always covers This project and its sub-projects

A person or group can have several roles on one project, never a role and No access there. In the API the place is named applies_to with the values organization, project and project-and-sub-projects (glossary: Where it counts).

Evaluation

For an actor and a place (the organization, or a project and its parents), from one port call that loads the actor's groups and the rows of the place and its parents:

  1. Default deny: nobody signed in reaches only public routes; a signed-in person without an applicable row can do nothing and sees no project (SEC-01).
  2. Applicable rows: the actor's own rows and their groups' rows for the whole organization; rows on a parent project with This project and its sub-projects; rows on the project itself.
  3. Rank: the depth of the row's project (the whole organization lowest, a top-level project 1, its sub-projects 2, …), and at equal depth the person's own row above a group's row.
  4. No access: the highest-ranked No access row removes every role row of equal or lower rank. Roles from higher up, roles of the person's groups on the same project and other groups' roles on the same project are removed; a role given lower down, or to the person directly where a group has No access, stays. Decide who has which role from a removed row is kept when the row is strictly above the No access (a parent project or the whole organization), so nobody is locked out by a project below them; from a row at the depth of a No access that removes it, it is not (ADR-0025, decision 6).
  5. Permissions: the union of the remaining roles' permissions that count at this place (organization permissions only at the organization and only from rows for the whole organization).
  6. Narrowing: for an access key, keep only the permissions of the key's kinds (or the picked permissions), and nothing outside the key's projects and their sub-projects; a key with projects gets nothing for the whole organization.
  7. Field mask: for each field of the catalogue and each remaining role, the level set for that role on the nearest of the project and its parents, else the role's own level; the mask is the highest of these (Hidden < Can see < Can change), at most Can see for a See only key.
  8. Who sees people: for each kind, the level set for each remaining role the same way; the viewer's level is the most open (Names > Role only > Hidden).
  9. Visibility (restricted issues SEC-05, V1): an issue is visible if the actor sees its project and (it isn't restricted or the actor is in one of its visibility groups).

The evaluation is cached for the request and never longer (review: the cache lives in the request context; tests sec_03_a_role_taken_away_counts_from_the_next_request, auth_07_a_key_follows_its_owner_losing_a_role_at_once).

The field catalogue

Declared once in bb-core (fields): key, name (message issue-field.<key>), the thing it belongs to, and the kind of people information when it holds a person. Own fields join in M3 (CF-06) through one key type, FieldKey: either a built-in field of this catalogue or an own field (FieldKey::Own(FieldId)), so levels, masks, the field-permission page, history and fields= name both the same way and no list of own fields is written twice. A new own field starts Can see for every role that sees the project and Can change for Team member and above; whoever makes it can change that at once. Levels per issue type use the lookup of ADR-0027.

KeyNameBelongs toHolds a person

A person in a field is shown only when the field is visible (mask) and then as its kind says (PersonRef).

Kinds of people information

Declared once in bb-core (people_kinds), each with its name (message people-kind.<key>): assigned-to, reported-by, last-changed-by, authors (comment and history authors), editing ("… is editing"), followers, time-entries, mentions, pictures (pictures of people: shown only where the kind of the place also gives Names), and project-members (member lists of a project, M2-Q3). The starting levels are in the table above; a new role starts with Hidden everywhere (default deny).

People who manage see names (M2-Q3): in Organization settings, Who has which role and Check access, a viewer who holds Manage people, Manage groups, Manage roles or Decide who has which role at that place sees names; anybody else sees the people in these screens by the kind Project members. E-mail addresses are never part of a PersonRef: only the person and holders of Manage people see them (ARCH-PERSON-REF finds others).

How PersonRef resolves

Every person in an answer is a PersonRef, resolved by bb-policy for the viewer, the kind and the place (ADR-0022). Enforced by: ARCH-PERSON-REF.

  1. The viewer themselves: their name.
  2. A removed person (PRIV-04, M9): with Names, the label Former user plus a random code (Former user K7Q2): four characters of Crockford Base32 from the secure random source, drawn again on a clash and longer when four run short, unique among removed people, made when the person is removed and stored with the tombstone, never made from the person's ID or a counter (PRIV-13); with Role only or Hidden, Someone.
  3. Anybody else by the viewer's level: Names → the name (and the ID, for links); Role only → the label of their first role at that place in the order of roles ("a Team member"), or Someone when they have none there; Hidden → Someone.
PersonRef = { shown: "name",    id: UserId, name: String }
          | { shown: "role",    role: String }          // the screen says "a {role}"
          | { shown: "someone" }
          | { shown: "former",  label: String }         // "K7Q2"; the screen says "Former user {label}"

A role label and Someone carry no ID, so a browser cannot tell two hidden people apart or follow one through the answers. A viewer who cannot see names for a kind cannot search, sort, group or filter by it (SEC-06, from M5 on).

The answer of Check access

A query use case (bb-app, WP-05) answers for a person and a place; the screen (WP-12) turns each reason into a sentence with message keys check-access.reason.<kind>. The checker holds Check access at that place; names follow the rule above.

CheckAccess = { person: PersonRef, place: Organization | ProjectRef,
                permissions: [{ permission, allowed: bool, reasons: [Reason] }],  // every permission that counts there
                fields:      [{ field, level, reasons: [Reason] }],
                people:      [{ kind, level, reasons: [Reason] }] }

Reason = { kind: "role",          role: RoleRef, through: Person | GroupRef, on: Place, applies_to, inherited: bool }
       | { kind: "no-access",     through: Person | GroupRef, on: Place }        // the row that removed the roles
       | { kind: "kept-above",    role: RoleRef, through: Person | GroupRef, on: Place }  // decide-roles kept over No access
       | { kind: "not-given",     roles: [RoleRef] }                              // the roles they have here; empty: none
       | { kind: "organization-only", role: RoleRef, on: Place }                  // counts only for the whole organization
       | { kind: "level",         role: RoleRef, level, set_on: Place | "role" }  // a field or people level and where it was set
Place  = "organization" | ProjectRef | "hidden"                                    // "hidden": a project the checker cannot see

Example: "Yes. Ana is in the group Backend, which has the role Team member in ACME. Website is inside ACME, so the role applies here too." comes from role with through: Backend, on: ACME, inherited: true. The decision always equals the engine's, and the reasons are enough to reach it (property test sec_03_check_access_explains_every_result_with_the_chain_of_reasons).

No counts that leak (PRIV-13)

  • No answer holds a number that counts things which include something the viewer cannot see: lists page with next_cursor and never answer a total; Used by counts only what the viewer can see; the project tree shows no counts of sub-projects or members; a member list that is Hidden for the viewer is left out with its number. Enforced by: ARCH-NO-COUNTERS (a total, count or similar property, or a whole number whose description says it counts, needs an entry in tools/checks/counter-exemptions.toml that says why the number holds only what the viewer can see; an entry that matches no property fails), and the tests priv_13_no_project_answer_holds_a_count and priv_13_used_by_counts_only_what_the_viewer_may_see.
  • No identifier counts up: people, groups, roles, projects, assignments and access keys have random IDs; Former user labels and access-key prefixes are random. Enforced by: ARCH-NO-COUNTERS (product code with a counting column or sequence, or a number made by adding one to a count, fails; only the folders named in the same file, the counting issue IDs of M3 and labels nobody sees, may).

Enforcement points

  • Every use case asks bb-policy first. Every result passes through Authorized<T>, which applies the field mask during serialization. The API answers a view only through answer_authorized or a page made by Page::of_authorized; the steps of signing in and the caller's own sign-in data, which hold nothing of anybody else, are the exceptions, each named with its reason in tools/checks/api-out-exemptions.toml. Enforced by: ARCH-AUTHZ-ONLY, ARCH-API-OUT (a handler that answers through answer(…) or axum::Json without an entry fails; an entry that nothing needs fails).
  • Every search gets the visibility predicate compiled into its SQL; the field catalogue given to the parser contains only readable fields (M5).
  • History, notifications, webhooks, exports, assistant context and live updates apply the receiver's mask and PersonRef (each in its milestone, with its SEC-MATRIX column).
  • Tests: a generated matrix (actors × routes, roles × fields × levels, roles × kinds × levels; the record names the entry point of each route, api today, and later entry points add theirs; the routes of issues and issue types are rows like any other, and their example requests make the issue a person has not reported) runs on every build. The route rows run the example request of every route of the API description (crates/bb-server/src/tests/matrix/examples.rs, one row per route, added in the change that adds the route) for nobody signed in, a person without a role, each starting role for the whole organization, a project lead on the parent project, a project lead on a sibling project only, No access on the project (and a lead above a No access) and, with the access keys of WP-09, a key that may only see and a key for another project; each answer is allowed or refused, and a refusal of what the person may not know about is resource.not_found, as for a project that does not exist. A route may answer a person without the permission with what they may see only when the table says so (the list of projects). The matrix writes what it covered to tools/checks/sec-matrix-record.txt and fails when the file differs; the check holds the file and the table against the API description. The rows of fields and of kinds of people information are tests of the engine (bb-policy, tests/engine/matrix.rs). Enforced by: SEC-MATRIX.

Data model

erDiagram
  PROJECT ||--o{ PROJECT : "contains"
  PROJECT ||--o{ ISSUE : has
  ISSUE ||--o{ ISSUE : "sub-issue of"
  ISSUE ||--o{ RELATION : from
  ISSUE ||--o{ RELATION : to
  RELATION }o--|| RELATION_KIND : "is a"
  ISSUE ||--o{ FIELD_VALUE : has
  FIELD ||--o{ FIELD_VALUE : defines
  ISSUE ||--o{ COMMENT : has
  ISSUE ||--o{ TIME_ENTRY : "booked on"
  PERSON ||--o{ TIME_ENTRY : books
  PERSON ||--o{ WORK_DAY : records
  WORK_DAY ||--o{ BREAK : has
  PROJECT ||--o{ FOLDER : has
  FOLDER ||--o{ DOCUMENT : has
  DOCUMENT ||--o{ DOCUMENT_VERSION : has
  BLOB ||--o{ ATTACHMENT : "stored as"
  BLOB ||--o{ DOCUMENT_VERSION : "file content"
  EVENT }o--|| PERSON : "caused by"
  • IDs: UUIDv7 everywhere internally; readable issue IDs per project, counting (WEB-142) or random (WEB-K7Q2X), with redirects from old IDs (ADR-0021); short names for projects.
  • Own fields (ADR-0006): one field_value table with typed columns (text, number, date, reference) and indexes per type; used by issues, time entries, work days, documents, releases and projects.
  • Relations: one table for every kind, including timeline dependencies; sub-issues use a parent column, shown as part of on the map.
  • Files: content-addressed blobs (SHA-256), referenced by attachments and document versions; deleted when nothing references them and no keep rule applies.
  • Time: all timestamps in UTC; each work day stores the person's time zone so "day" means their day.
  • Versions: every changeable entity has a version number for optimistic locking.
  • Edit locks: edit_lock rows (what, who, session, token, expires at) for long text and admin editors; private drafts in edit_draft; both deleted when no longer needed (ADR-0019).
  • Deleted items move to the trash (soft delete with a deletion date), then are removed by the keep-and-delete job.

Events, history and the outbox (ADR-0007)

Every change appends a domain event in the same transaction: who (actor), how (UI, API, MCP, assistant), what (entity, field changes before → after), why (reason, when required). The outbox delivers events to consumers that run after commit:

ConsumerUses events to …
Historyshow the change log (filtered by the reader's field mask)
Notificationsnotify followers and mentioned people (filtered per recipient)
Webhookssend signed payloads (filtered by the bot account's permissions)
Security logappend hash-chained entries for security-relevant events
Full-text indexupdate search text (inside the same database)
Live updatestell open screens that something changed (built last)

Consumers are idempotent and resume from their last position after a restart.

In bb-store: Database::record_change is the only way to write domain data: it runs the change, appends the event and the outbox entry, and commits all three or none. Outbox positions are handed out from a counter row that the change transaction locks until it commits, so positions become visible in order and a consumer that has seen position 7 cannot miss a 6 that commits later (the price: changes commit one after the other). Each consumer stores the last position it finished (outbox_done). Enforced by: the event tests of bb-store; ARCH-EVENTS (a command use case in bb-app must write through the ChangeStore port, whose method record_change bb-store implements); ARCH-SQL-EDGE (no other crate may write to the database).

Background jobs (ADR-0017) are rows in the job table. A worker leases due jobs with one UPDATE … RETURNING statement (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED on PostgreSQL); a lease that runs out puts the job back, every start counts as an attempt, failures wait 30 seconds doubled each time (at most an hour), and after the last attempt the job goes to the dead-letter list, which an administrator can requeue. Enforced by: the job tests of bb-store.

The security log (SEC-15) is append-only. Each entry stores the HMAC-SHA256 (under the log key, keys/log.key) of the previous entry's hash and all its own fields in a length-prefixed encoding. Because the key is not in the database, somebody who can only change the database (SQL injection, a stolen copy) cannot change an entry and hash the rest of the chain again; somebody who also holds the host's key files can, and that is outside what the log protects against. After every append, one line seq hash signature goes to an append-only anchor file outside the database (logs/security-head.log, owner-only). verify_security_log reads one consistent snapshot (no write lock) and reports the first entry that does not verify (a gap, a broken link, changed content, a missing or forged checkpoint, an anchor line with a wrong signature) and whether the database reaches the newest anchored entry with the same hash (cut off or replaced ends are Truncated); a log whose anchor file is missing verifies but says it is not anchored. After the keep period, whole blocks of 1000 entries are deleted from the start; before deleting, the job verifies those blocks from the previous checkpoint and that the first kept entry points to the last deleted hash, in the same transaction, and refuses otherwise. A checkpoint is left: place, hash and time of the deletion, signed with the log key, so the remaining entries still verify. The newest entry is never deleted. Network addresses are stored shortened (IPv4 /24, IPv6 /48). Enforced by: the hash-chain property tests (sec_15_any_changed_row_breaks_the_chain, sec_15_a_rewritten_tail_without_the_key_does_not_verify) and the security-log tests of bb-store.

Storage types: every whole number is a BIGINT, every moment is microseconds since 1970 in a BIGINT, IDs are 16-byte blobs and JSON is text, so both databases hand back the same Rust types. SQLite runs in WAL mode with foreign keys on, a busy timeout and synchronous=FULL (a committed change survives a power cut; the cost is one more disk flush per commit than NORMAL), and every write transaction starts with BEGIN IMMEDIATE (one writer at a time). Migrations record a checksum of their steps and take the write lock (SQLite) or an advisory lock (PostgreSQL), reading the record again inside the transaction, so two processes starting together cannot apply one migration twice; a changed, renamed or unknown applied migration stops the start. PostgreSQL pools are sized to the number of processors. Every table is the home of an entity with personal-data marks. Enforced by: DATA-MARKS (tables), DATA-MIGRATIONS and ARCH-DB-PARITY (the migrations test and every repository test run on both databases).

Privacy engineering (ADR-0015)

  • Every stored field is marked in the entity definition: personal data or not, category (contact, employee time, content, technical), and the legal basis note. Unmarked fields fail the build.
  • The marks generate: Download my data, the Remove a person plan, keep-and-delete jobs, the record of processing, and the data-flow map.
  • Logs hold IDs, never names or e-mail addresses; IP addresses are kept 7 days by default.
  • Former users: a removed person becomes a tombstone (Former user K7Q2); references stay valid, personal data is gone.
  • Legal holds: working hours stay until their keep period ends, even after a person is removed.

Search language (ADR-0005)

Grammar sketch (final grammar is part of milestone work):

search     = [ expr ] [ "sort by" sort ("," sort)* ]
expr       = term ( ("and" | "or") term )*
term       = "not" term | "(" expr ")" | condition
condition  = field op value | field "contains" text | helper
op         = "is" | "is not" | "<" | ">" | "<=" | ">=" | "in" | "within"
helper     = "connected to" key [ "within" n "steps" ] | "under" key | "blocks" key | …
value      = word | quoted | number | date | "me" | "today" | "in last" n unit
  • The printer writes a canonical form; parse(print(tree)) == tree is a property test.
  • Simple search edits the same tree; anything without a picker becomes an editable text button.

Settings and configuration (ADR-0018)

  • Start-up settings (address, port, data folder, database URL, certificates): bugaboo.toml or environment variables, written by the setup wizard.
  • Everything else comes from one settings registry: each setting is defined once (key, type, default, levels — organization / project / person — who may change it, help text key). The registry drives storage, the API and the settings dialogs, so a new setting appears in the UI without hand-written forms.
  • In code: settings are declared in crates/bb-core/src/settings/catalog.rs and nowhere else, and are read through their typed handle (settings::APPEARANCE_MODE). A setting key written as text elsewhere, in Rust or in the browser app, is a way around the registry and is found (not in generated files, in migrations, or as the argument of a message lookup: messages and settings are separate namespaces, and appearance.larger-text is both); the browser app names a setting through the generated constants of @bugaboo/api-client (settingKeys), and a migration may name the keys of its time. Enforced by: ARCH-SETTINGS.
  • What the registry knows: key, name and explanation (message keys), type, bounds or list limits, a format for text (a fixed list of choices with the words for each, a time zone, the address of a page of the app, the keys of shortcuts), the levels, who may change it (changed_by) and whether it can be locked. One check of a value (SettingDefinition::accepts) is used by the store and the use cases. Settings that exist only for tests (feature test-settings of bb-core) cover the project level while no real setting is set on a project.
  • Layers (CFG-06): the value that counts is the default, then the organization's, then the nearest project up the tree that sets it, then the person's own; a value the organization locked wins over every lower layer and lower layers are refused with setting.locked (decided inside the change, so a lock made at the same moment is seen). Reset to default takes the value of one layer away and leaves the others. Every answer says where the value comes from (default, organization, from ACME, your own) and whether it is locked. One function, Layers::resolve, decides; the store, the use cases and the tests use it.
  • Who may change what (ADR-0025, decision 14): the organization's layer needs Change organization settings; a project's layer Change project settings in that project (a setting only administrators change also needs the organization's permission); a person's own layer is theirs alone and only for a setting each person changes. Every change writes its event, and a setting of the topics security and auth also a security-log entry. Enforced by: the tests cfg_06_only_administrators_change_organization_values_and_each_person_only_their_own and cfg_06_a_change_of_a_setting_that_touches_security_is_in_the_security_log, ARCH-EVENTS and ARCH-PERMS.
  • A person's own values are stored for that person (their own table, person_setting, so the person is a column with a personal-data mark), are never kept by the browser or a cache (x-never-stored), and are gone with the person. The routes are one set for every setting: /settings, /projects/{id}/settings and /me/settings, and the browser draws any topic from them with one generic form.

User interface

  • Server data: only in the TanStack Query cache. URL: the search, the presentation and the open issue live in typed URL parameters, so every screen is shareable.
  • Lean requests: each screen asks for the fields its layout shows (?fields=); lists use cursor pagination and are virtualized.
  • Text: every user-facing string is a key in messages/en.json (ICU message format), typed via generated keys. The hooks reject literal text in components. The browser catalog is split into parts (ADR-0028): the first page loads shared, and the entry of each feature imports its own part, so the texts of a lazy area arrive with its chunk; t() of a text whose part is not loaded fails. Enforced by: TXT-CATALOG, DOC-GENERATED.
  • Text in Rust: the server uses the constants and functions generated into bb_core::message (SERVER_NOT_FOUND, server_port_busy(port)), whose placeholders are typed arguments; a key that does not exist does not compile. Keys that nothing uses are found. Enforced by: TXT-CATALOG.
  • Styles: one theme file (design/theme.kdl): tokens per theme and mode, and the rules of every component as part rules that use token variables only; one generated style sheet; no inline styles and no class names (CSP, THEME-ONLY).
  • Accessibility: React Aria Components for focus, keyboard and screen-reader behavior; axe checks in CI.

Errors

  • One ErrorCode enum in bb-core (for example issue.not_found, issue.version_conflict, search.unknown_field). The message of a code is made from its text, never written next to it: error.<area>.<name> with - for _ (auth.wrong_credentials is error.auth.wrong-credentials). The same rule gives permission.<key>, permission-topic.<topic>, starting-role.<key>, people-kind.<key>, issue-field.<key>, field-level.<word> and people-level.<word> (words! with messages, bb-core). A made key that is not in the message catalog stops the build (bb-core, tests/message_keys.rs), for any enum that is declared with messages. Enforced by: the build itself, ARCH-ERRORS and ARCH-PERMS (they read the enums and hold the keys to the rules of errors and permissions), and TXT-CATALOG (a made key counts as used, so a key nothing makes is found).
  • The API answers with application/problem+json: type, title, status, code, message_key, params and the request_id (the same as the x-request-id header). Handlers take their input through ApiJson, ApiQuery and ApiPath, whose rejections are problem+json, and return an ApiError made from an ErrorCode; a failure below /api that still has no problem body (any layer) is turned into one by its status: the status, the title and the message key come from the table, and a cause inside the server goes to the log (ApiError::internal), never into the answer. Every route in the OpenAPI document lists the standard answers 429, 500 and 503. Enforced by: ARCH-ERRORS (finds error answers built from a text written in the code, handlers that use axum::Json, Query, Path or Form as extractors instead of the wrappers, and compares the generated API description with the table).
  • The Display texts of error types such as TlsError are English in code and reach only the log or the terminal; a person reads catalogue messages. Enforced by: ARCH-ERRORS (an error answer cannot be made from a text).
  • A stale version has an answer of its own (edit.version_changed, ADR-0019 amendment M3): the problem body also holds conflict with the version the record has now, who changed it last (a PersonRef for the reader, of the kind Last changed by), when, which fields, and the values those fields have now. The values are left out for a field the reader's role hides. A use case only answers AppError::Stale (the record, where it sits, who asks); AuthApi makes the Conflict from the last event of the record in one place, and bb-api writes it into the answer and documents it as the 409 of every route that takes a version, so a route carries it without code of its own. The browser writes the sentence from it ("Ben changed Priority to Critical 2 minutes ago."): the message itself has no placeholder. Enforced by: ARCH-VERSIONED (a route that takes a version documents the conflict), TEST-EDIT-LOCKS (iss_17_a_stale_version_answers_who_changed_what).
  • The TypeScript client gets the codes as a union type; the UI shows the message from the catalog.
  • An error message in the catalog has no placeholder, so an error cannot carry a name or number the person may not see; anything hidden answers with resource.not_found, exactly as if it did not exist. Enforced by: ARCH-ERRORS.

Observability

  • Structured JSON logs (tracing, one object per line on standard error) with random request IDs. One line per request holds the request ID, method, route pattern, status, duration and the client network cut short (IPv4 /24, IPv6 /48); never the path as typed, the query, headers, bodies, names, e-mail addresses or free text. Enforced by: DATA-LOGS.
  • Health endpoints: /health/live answers while the process runs; /health/ready also checks the data folder (and the database once the store exists) and answers 503 when something is missing; both are sent with Cache-Control: no-store; optional Prometheus metrics, off by default and protected.
  • The admin Status page shows version, database, disk, jobs, backups and certificate expiry.

Performance

  • Per-request caches for permission evaluation; Brotli and gzip compression (see Compression under Browser protections).
  • Lean lists (PERF-02): every list takes fields, cursor and limit, written once in bb-api (lean.rs, paging.rs, seal.rs). fields names what the screen shows; the answer schema lists every field that can be asked for, and the route names a small default, never everything (one table of fields per route, each marked as default or not). A field that does not exist and one the person may not read are refused alike with request.unknown_field (SEC-06). A page holds at most the page size of bb-core (paging, the one definition for the use cases and for the API description) and every page answers next_cursor: the cursor of the next page, null on the last. Enforced by: ARCH-LEAN (the parameters, the maximum of limit and next_cursor in the API description), backed by the tests perf_02_a_list_answers_only_the_fields_asked_for, perf_02_a_list_refuses_an_unknown_field_like_a_hidden_one and perf_02_every_page_answers_next_cursor_and_the_last_one_answers_null.
  • Cursors: a cursor is opaque text: the position of the last item (sort key and ID) with a tag made by HMAC-SHA256 under a random key that is made when the server starts and kept in memory only, and bound to the list it was made for. A cursor that was changed, cut, made up, taken from another list or made before a restart answers request.bad_cursor, whatever is inside it. A cursor holds only a position: every filter and every permission comes from the request, every time. A cursor is readable (the seal is a checksum, not a lock), so it never carries a value the person may not see: its position is made of the last item of the page, which the person has just been shown, never of something a page looked at and left out (a project they may not know about, a person they may not see). A page that stops after looking at many hidden items continues past them with a number of whole stretches that were looked at (the project list of the access-key form: NAME, NAME+500 or +500), which says no more than that the page ended early and there is more. Enforced by: the test auth_07_the_cursor_of_the_projects_for_a_key_holds_no_name_of_a_project_hidden_from_the_person, and review for every other list (each list says in its use case what its position is made of; the lists of invitations and of a person's own keys use the last item they return); the tests perf_02_paging_walks_every_item_once_and_refuses_a_changed_cursor and perf_02_a_cursor_that_is_cut_empty_made_up_or_for_another_list_is_refused, and review (that no route puts a filter or a permission into a cursor).
  • Who asks comes before what is asked: a list judges the person (401, 403) before its query (400), so a person who cannot list learns nothing about its fields or cursors. Enforced by: the test perf_02_a_list_judges_who_asks_before_it_judges_the_query.
  • References, not embedded objects: a list item names a related thing by its ID, or by a reference schema whose name ends in Ref (PersonRef); it embeds the thing only when the route declares the query parameter include with the closed set of names that may be embedded, and declares include only when it embeds. Enforced by: ARCH-LEAN (an embedded object without include, and include without an embedded object), and review (whether a property is "another resource" is a judgment).
  • ETags and 304 (PERF-03): a read that holds no personal data gets a weak ETag, a tag made with the seal of this server run from the final answer body after masking, so two people with different rights never share a tag for different text; If-None-Match with the current tag answers 304 without a body. Every GET documents the ETag header and the 304 answer, except the routes marked x-never-stored. Enforced by: ARCH-LEAN, backed by the test perf_03_every_get_answers_an_etag_and_304_on_a_match, which runs over every GET route of the API description.
  • Cache rules in one place: bb-api (etag.rs) sets them for every answer below /api, from the route table permissions::ROUTES (the same table puts x-permission, x-never-stored and x-secret into the API description; no handler writes a mark by hand) and from the answer itself. A read is Cache-Control: private, no-cache (kept, asked again every time). An answer with personal data (a GET route marked x-never-stored: who is signed in, the sessions, the invitations, the second step, the state of the server, the projects a person sees and one project, which differ with what the person may see) is no-store with no ETag. An answer that hands out a secret (a route the route table declares Secret, marked x-secret, or any answer that sets a cookie) is no-store, has no ETag and is marked as a secret answer, which the compression never touches (Compression under Browser protections). Every other answer, errors included, is no-store; an answer too big to tag is passed on whole as no-store. An answer that clears the session cookie also sends Clear-Site-Data: "cache". A new route has a row in the table with the kind of its answer (Ordinary, NeverStored or Secret), so nobody forgets to decide. Enforced by: the tests perf_03_only_a_read_is_never_stored_and_every_read_is_ordinary_or_never_stored, perf_03_a_route_whose_answer_has_a_field_named_like_a_secret_is_declared_a_secret, perf_03_answers_with_a_secret_are_not_stored_or_compressed, perf_03_no_route_that_hands_out_a_secret_is_compressed, perf_03_answers_with_personal_data_are_never_stored_for_anybody and sec_12_signing_out_clears_what_the_browser_cached.
  • Files of the app: named by their content hash and sent public, max-age=31536000, immutable; the start page and other files are no-cache. The manifest the build leaves for the checks is neither in the binary nor served. Enforced by: the tests perf_03_files_with_a_content_hash_are_kept_forever_and_api_answers_are_asked_again and perf_04_what_the_build_leaves_for_the_checks_is_not_served.
  • Compression quality: one number, in tools/dev/compression.json, read by the server and by the budget check, so the check measures what a browser receives. Enforced by: the tests perf_04_the_server_compresses_with_the_quality_the_budget_is_measured_with and the_budget_is_measured_with_the_quality_the_server_compresses_with (xtask).
  • First page budget (PERF-04): the JavaScript the first route loads (the entry and what it imports at once, read from the Vite manifest) stays within the budget in tools/checks/perf-bundle.toml, the only place the number is written. The WebAssembly modules of the build have a budget of their own in the same file, measured with the same Brotli quality (follow-up M2-F03), because every browser that opens a preview or an editor fetches them. Enforced by: PERF-BUNDLE.
  • SQLite: WAL mode, one writer task with a queue, many readers. PostgreSQL: a pool sized to CPU count.
  • A dataset generator (cargo xtask dataset --issues 1000000) feeds benchmarks in CI; budgets from PERF-01…06 fail the build when exceeded.

AI (ADR-0013)

  • Providers: one trait; adapters for Anthropic, OpenAI-compatible endpoints (which cover local models) and a test fake.
  • Context builder: reads as the actor, drops hidden and AI-excluded fields, wraps people's text in clearly fenced "untrusted content" blocks.
  • Tool registry: shared with MCP. In the assistant, write tools return proposals; nothing changes without Apply.
  • Output: rendered by the Markdown renderer with remote images and auto-links disabled; marked Written with the assistant when saved.
  • Hard rules (AI Act): no tools that rank, evaluate or assign people; no access to working hours; no mood analysis. These tools don't exist, so they can't be called.
  • Limits: per-person and organization budgets; each call logged with metadata (who, tool, size, cost), not content, unless an admin enables content logging for troubleshooting.

Technical debt we accept on purpose

  • No real-time co-editing in 1.0. Instead: edit locks with heartbeats for long text, drafts that are never lost, and confirmed saves (ADR-0019).
  • Live updates come last; until then, screens refresh on focus and after own changes.
  • The served model's control plane starts minimal (scripts plus the operator API) and grows when there are customers.

Architecture checks

The architecture is only true if the code follows it. AI agents write most of the code, so every rule that a machine can check is checked, by many small checks rather than one big one (ADR-0020).

How it works

flowchart LR
  cat["tools/checks/catalog.toml<br/>every check, once"]
  xt["cargo xtask check …<br/>implements every entry"]
  edit["Claude Code hook<br/>after each file edit"]
  commit["lefthook<br/>commit · push"]
  ci["CI<br/>all · nightly · release"]
  cat --> xt
  edit --> xt
  commit --> xt
  ci --> xt
  • One catalogue, one runner. Each check has an ID (for example ARCH-AUTHZ-ONLY), a plain title, the rule it enforces, the tool, when it runs and which files trigger it. People, agents and CI all run the same code.
  • Small and fast. A check runs only when its files change, and the selected checks run side by side, as many at once as the machine has cores (several read the whole repository, so one after the other they grow with the code). Edit-time checks take under 3 seconds per file and commit-time checks under 10 seconds on a quiet PC, so nobody is tempted to skip them.
  • Explains itself. A failing check prints one sentence: what's wrong, which rule, and where it's written down.

Groups of checks

GroupGuards
FMTFormatting: rustfmt, oxfmt (TypeScript, JSON, CSS), taplo (TOML), rumdl (Markdown)
LINTLinting: clippy, oxlint with type-aware tsgolint (TypeScript 7), stylelint, tsc type check, typos, lychee, actionlint
TXT / STYPlain words and design: no literal UI text, message catalog complete, glossary "don't say" words, tokens only, theme contrast

SECSecrets, private details of the owner, dangerous patterns, the permission matrix, security headers, known vulnerabilities
DATAPersonal-data marks, no personal data in logs, one schema source

PERF / TESTBundle and WebAssembly budgets, query counts, benchmarks, accessibility, search round trip, edit locks
METAThe checks themselves (next section)

The full list, generated from the catalogue, follows this chapter.

Checks that guard the checks

Adding a rule should be easy, and forgetting part of it impossible. The META checks make sure that:

  1. Catalogue and implementation match (META-CATALOG): no check without an entry, no entry without a check.
  2. Every check is tested (META-FIXTURES): each has a "bad" example that must fail and a "good" example that must pass, in tools/checks/fixtures/<ID>/.
  3. Nothing is unchecked (META-COVERAGE): every file type in the repository is covered by a formatter or linter. Adding the first .sql, .yaml or .py file fails until a check covers it. This is the hook that asks for new hooks. Generated files need no check of their own; the few other exceptions are listed with a reason in tools/checks/coverage-exemptions.toml.
  4. New modules are declared first (META-NEW-MODULE): a new crate, package or top-level folder needs a module-map entry and dependency rules.
  5. Every rule is traceable (META-RULE-TRACE): each "must" in the coding standards, decision records and these chapters names its check ID or says review with a reason.
  6. Callers agree (META-WIRING): lefthook, the Claude Code hooks and CI call only xtask, with the same lists.
  7. Suppressions are visible (META-SUPPRESS): every allow, oxlint-disable, ast-grep ignore or "not affected" vulnerability statement needs a reason and an issue ID, and the total can't grow unnoticed. The file types searched are listed in xtask/src/checks/meta_suppress.rs.
  8. Checks stay fast (META-SPEED). The 3 and 10 seconds hold on a quiet PC. Several builds often run at once, and wall-clock time alone would then fail a fast check, so the check times a fixed reference workload (a few small processes plus some file and CPU work, like a typical check) right before, during and right after each measurement. The budget is a multiple of that reference: the quiet-PC budget times how much longer the reference took than on a quiet PC (the load factor, never below 1 and never above 20). Each timing is taken up to 3 times and the best attempt counts, which drops one-off spikes. A check that is slow by itself is slow in every attempt and still fails. The failure names the measured time, the allowed time, the reference time and the load factor, so a human can tell real slowness from load. The numbers (budgets, quiet reference, attempts, ceiling) are defined once, in xtask/src/checks/meta_speed.rs.

Adding a rule

  1. Write the rule where it belongs (coding standards, a decision record, or a chapter here), with Enforced by: <ID>.
  2. Add the entry to tools/checks/catalog.toml.
  3. Implement it in xtask/src/checks/.
  4. Add the bad and good examples.

The META checks fail until all four steps are done.

Database tests

Every repository test runs against SQLite and PostgreSQL (ADR-0003). Nothing is installed machine-wide (ADR-0024).

  • PostgreSQL 18.6 is a pinned tool in tools/dev/tools.toml. On Windows cargo xtask setup downloads the official binaries (checksum checked) into .tools/postgresql/. On Linux it uses the system PostgreSQL (on the PATH, or under /usr/lib/postgresql/*/bin as on GitHub's Ubuntu runners) and explains how to install it when missing.
  • cargo xtask db start | stop | reset | url manages a throwaway cluster in .tools/pg-data/. It listens on 127.0.0.1 only, on the port postgres from tools/dev/ports.json (strict: a busy port is an error). Its random password lives in .tools/pg-password, never in the repository; on Windows the file is protected only by the inherited permissions of your user profile, on Unix it is readable by its owner only. All work folders share port 47240 (ADR-0023), so only one cargo xtask ci or db start runs at a time on a machine. db url prints the connection URL for tools of your own.
  • cargo xtask db run -- <command> starts the cluster if needed, runs the command with BB_TEST_DATABASES=sqlite,postgres, BB_TEST_POSTGRES_URL and BB_DB_PARITY_FILE set, stops the cluster again if it started it (also after an error), and then checks the parity record against ARCH-DB-PARITY and DATA-MIGRATIONS. Before the run it deletes the old record and any bbtest_* databases left behind by killed test programs; after a failure it deletes the record again, so an old or partial record never decides anything. cargo xtask ci runs the Rust tests this way.
  • Writing a test: bb_testing::each_database("name", async |db| { … }).await runs the body once per selected database. The body gets a typed pool (db.pool() is Pool::Sqlite or Pool::Postgres; tests/example_repository.rs in bb-testing shows the pattern). Each run gets an empty database of its own (a temporary file for SQLite, a freshly created and afterwards dropped database for PostgreSQL), so tests never see each other's data. Without BB_TEST_DATABASES, plain cargo test runs SQLite only.
  • The record target/db-parity.txt has one line per finished run (<database> <test name>). ARCH-DB-PARITY fails when a test ran on one database but not the other, or when a database did not run at all. DATA-MIGRATIONS additionally forbids .sql migration files and, once bb-store has migrations, wants its migrations test in the record for both databases. Both rules on the record run only inside cargo xtask db run, right after the tests; check all never reads a record left on disk (it can be from an older state of the code). There, ARCH-DB-PARITY checks that cargo xtask ci runs the Rust tests through db run, and DATA-MIGRATIONS checks for .sql files.

Enforced by: ARCH-DB-PARITY, DATA-MIGRATIONS.

Sample organization

A realistic, fully fictional organization used for development, end-to-end tests, demos and the optional "try it out" mode (OPS-12). Generated by cargo xtask dataset sample, deterministic from a seed (default 42), into SQLite or PostgreSQL. The people and the organization take a few seconds; the 10,000 issues with their comments take about six minutes (see Issues of the sample below), which is why --check and cargo xtask dev --sample make a smaller one.

Making it and using it

cargo xtask dataset sample [--seed N] [--database sqlite|postgres] [--issues N] [--out <folder>] [--check] runs the bb-sample program (crate bb-sample, architecture §4) as a process, so xtask does not link the store or the use cases. The program makes the organization through the same use cases the API calls: the first administrator with the setup code, everybody else as that administrator by invitation, so every change has its event and its security log entry and nothing is written to the database by hand. It is deterministic from the seed (default 42) with its own random source; it never reads the clock, because every date comes from one start moment that xtask passes in (now; a fixed moment for --check). On SQLite it takes a few seconds.

  • Names: the folders the sample is made in, the names of its files and the environment variable of the PostgreSQL address are written once, in tools/dev/sample.json; xtask, the bb-sample program and the end-to-end tests all read that file.
  • What it makes in <out> (default target/sample, target/sample-postgres on PostgreSQL): data/ is a data folder that bugaboo serve --data-dir can start on (copy it first); sign-in.txt has one line per person (e-mail address, random password, role, name, the secret of the code app for the few people who have one, and the access key for the three who have one; the columns are separated by tabs, an empty column stays empty); dump.json is the canonical dump; sample.json marks the folder as made by the tool, so the next run may empty it and a folder with anything else in it is left alone. The passwords are random for every run and come from the operating system, never from the seed: no password is in the repository, and sign-in.txt is the only file that holds one (in target/, which Git ignores).
  • On PostgreSQL the program uses an empty database in the throwaway cluster of cargo xtask db (started and stopped by the command when needed). The address goes to the program in the environment variable BB_SAMPLE_DATABASE_URL, never on its command line.
  • People and organization: 50 fictional people with the mix of roles below, recorded in the plan (roster) and in the dump. After the people, bb_sample::Organization (the one filling of the extension point bb_sample::Later) makes the groups, the custom roles, the projects with their sub-projects and every row of Who has which role, as the first administrator, through the use cases of M2 (a change every second of the sample's clock, so the records come in the same order every time). Each person also chose a time zone and how dates and numbers are written, as they do in My settings, and a few have an access key. Names come from crates/bb-sample/data/names.toml, written for Bugaboo (no third-party name data); every address is under bugaboo.example. The people the demos name are the same whatever the seed: Ada Brandt (the administrator who runs the demo), Ana Moreno (a Contributor, on Website through the group External and nowhere else) and Ben Hale (a Team member for the whole organization, with No access on Android). The names of the groups, projects and custom roles are written once, in tools/dev/sample.json, which the program, xtask and the end-to-end tests read.
  • Issues of the sample (M3 WP-11): after the organization, bb_sample::Everything (the filling of the extension point that bb-sample runs) makes the issues of Projects below: the starting issue types and kinds of relation, how each project gives out its IDs, the own fields Severity, Platforms and Customer, the groups of labels and the labels, then every issue, sub-issue, tag, label, status change, relation and comment (some edited), and at the end one edit lock held and one draft waiting. All of it goes through the use cases, one change at a time, by the Administrators and Team members of the whole organization, each signed in on the working days they work (Monday to Friday, from nine, the clock of the sample running through eighteen months), so every date is a working day and every issue has a person who made it. The plan (crates/bb-sample/src/issues_plan.rs) has no database in it: it is worked out from the seed and the counts of tools/dev/sample.json (issues: the full count, the small count, the share of each type, of each project and place, the own fields, labels and tags, the numbers of relations and comments), and its words are in crates/bb-sample/data/issues.toml. --issues N scales every count to N issues (the full sample is issues.total, 10,000; --check and cargo xtask dev --sample make issues.smallTotal, 500). The readable IDs of the projects with Random IDs are the only thing that differs from run to run, and the dump leaves them out. No issue is restricted, and there are no releases. The history of every issue is read from the events at the end (what the daily job history.catch-up does), so the first page that shows one does not have to. The program is built with optimisations for this, as it runs about seventy thousand use cases: the full sample takes about six minutes on SQLite (the people and the organization, three seconds), the small one twenty seconds. Enforced by: TEST-SAMPLE-DATA (the dump of every --check run holds the numbers of the plan).
  • Using it in browser tests: cargo xtask dev --sample makes a fresh sample and starts the server on it (it prints where sign-in.txt is). A file of end-to-end tests that says test.use({ sample: true }) gets a server on a fresh copy of target/sample/data (one server per Playwright worker, ADR-0023 ports) and reads the people from samplePeople() (web/app/e2e/support/sample.ts). cargo xtask ci makes the sample before the browser tests; by hand, run cargo xtask dataset sample first. The M1 tests of setup and signing in still start from an empty data folder.
  • The check: cargo xtask dataset sample --check makes the organization twice on SQLite and twice on PostgreSQL from one seed into target/sample-check/ and compares the canonical dumps. The dump leaves out what is random by design (IDs, password hashes, secrets and the hashes of the security log) and replaces each ID by a label that counts the records of a kind in the order they appear (person#3), so it still says which events and entries are about the same record. The run fails when two dumps differ, when an address is not under bugaboo.example, when a name is not a given name and a family name of the list, or when a password, secret or access key of sign-in.txt is found in any other file of a run (the database, the keys, the log files, the dump, what the program said). The dump also holds a part issues: for each project the issues of each type, status and priority, the sub-issues, the relations of each kind with the longest chain of blocks and the number of circles, tags, labels, the values of each own field, the comments (and how many were edited) and the locks and drafts left behind, and the run fails when they are not the plan of tools/dev/sample.json scaled to the issues asked for, within issues.tolerancePercent (IssuePlan::problems in bb-dev-words, which the tests of bb-sample ask as well). The dump also holds the groups with their members, the roles with how many people hold each, the projects with their leads, every row of Who has which role and the levels projects and custom roles set; the run fails when a group or project of this section is missing, when a role of the mix below is missing or held by another number of people, or when a project has no Project lead. The rules and their failing and passing examples are in xtask/src/checks/test_sample_data.rs and tools/checks/fixtures/TEST-SAMPLE-DATA/.

Enforced by: TEST-SAMPLE-DATA (cargo xtask ci runs it), ARCH-HTTP-EDGE (bb-sample is the second crate that may wire an adapter), SEC-SECRETS (no password in the repository).

People (50) and groups

  • 2 Administrators, 4 Project leads, 30 Team members, 8 Contributors, 4 Viewers, 2 Guests, plus 1 bot account (bot accounts come with AUTH-08, M12).
  • Groups: Backend, Frontend, Mobile, QA, Support, Docs, Management, External. Every Team member is in one of the first six, every Viewer in Management and four Contributors (Ana is the first) in External.
  • Who has which role (made in M2, shown by Check access): the second Administrator and 18 of the 30 Team members for the whole organization; the other 12 Team members only through the groups Backend, Frontend, Mobile, QA and Docs (a group gives its role on its projects); the Viewers through Management for the whole organization; the Contributors in External on Website, the other four on Mobile app and Operations; the Guests one each on Website and Mobile app; one Project lead for each of the four projects; and one No access (Ben Hale on Android).
  • Two custom roles: Support agent (a Team member without Cost center, given to the group Support on Operations) and Security reviewer (needs two-step sign-in; the five people who have a code app hold it on Operations).
  • Cost center is hidden from Contributors, and Guests see no authors or mentions, on Mobile app; Website keeps the starting rules, so the M2 exit demo has something to change.
  • Generated names from a mixed international name list; e-mail addresses under the reserved domain bugaboo.example, so nothing can ever reach a real inbox.
  • Each person has a time zone, some have passkeys, two-step sign-in or access keys. Two people are already removed (Former user labels) to test GDPR flows.

What's inside

  • Issues over the last 18 months (dates are shifted at generation time, so the data always looks current): Bug 45 %, Task 30 %, Feature 20 %, Goal 5 %; realistic status ages, priorities and labels; own fields (Severity, Platforms, Customer); about 2 % restricted issues.
  • Sub-issues under goals, and about 3,000 relations of every kind, including chains deeper than four steps and one deliberate blocks circle (to test the warning).
  • Releases: three per project, one in the past, one current, one planned.
  • Comments: about 30,000, with mentions; some edited.
  • Files and documents: about 500 small generated attachments (images, PDFs), 60 pages and 20 files with several versions each.
  • Time: about 20,000 time entries with activities and cost centers, six months of working hours for every employee (including some broken working-time rules), and a few running timers.
  • Configuration: workflows for each issue type, field permissions (for example Cost center hidden from Contributors), Who sees people set for Guests, fields excluded from AI, saved searches, dashboards, two custom themes.
  • States worth testing: an edit lock held by someone, a pending conflict, a closed month, a person with a removal in progress.

The M2 exit demo on the sample

web/app/e2e/m2-exit-demo.spec.ts runs it in cargo xtask ci, on a phone and a computer, with axe in the four themes at every step; with BB_SCREENSHOT_DIR set the same run takes the pictures of the review page (M2/demo/<step>-<phone|computer>-<light|dark>.png). By hand, with cargo xtask dev --sample (it prints where sign-in.txt is; sign in as Ada Brandt, the first line):

  1. Organization settings › Roles & permissions: make the role Reviewer from a copy of Viewer and tick See how the server is doing.
  2. Website › Project settings › Field permissions: for Contributor set Cost center to Hidden. Mobile app has it hidden already; Shop and Blog show it hidden "from Website".
  3. Website › Project settings › Who sees people: for Guest set Assigned to to Hidden; the preview now says Someone.
  4. Website › Project settings › Check access: pick Ana Moreno and read why she is a Contributor (through the group External) and that Cost center is hidden from her. Pick Ben Hale in Android to read that No access wins over his role.
  5. Sign out; sign in as the Guest of Website (see dump.json, the row with the role Guest on WEB) and as Ana: the tree shows Website with its sub-projects only, and the settings pages and Mobile app are not found.

Large dataset

cargo xtask dataset large --issues 1000000 builds the same shape at the PERF scale (500 people, 500 projects) for benchmarks.

Ten people at the same time

Concurrency is tested with 10 simulated people (an administrator and Team members of one project, made for the run), each in their own browser context (Playwright) or API client (cargo xtask load --people 10):

ScenarioWhat must hold
Three people try to edit the same descriptionOne gets the lock; the others see "… is editing"; Edit anyway moves the lock and keeps the first person's draft
Two people change the status of the same issue within a secondOne wins; the other sees the conflict message; nothing is half-saved
A lock holder's network dropsThe lock frees itself within a minute; their text is kept as a draft and offered with Compare and save
Ten people change different fields of one issueAll ten changes land (whoever was second presses Use mine); one event for each; the version counts up ten times
Changing many issues while somebody edits one of themA lock covers only the long text, so the issue under edit changes too, and the editor's save lands afterwards with no conflict note (the status is another field); an issue whose text was saved after the preview is skipped and named, and the others change
Everyone drags cards on the same boardFinal board matches the event log; every person's screen shows the final state after refresh
Timers and working hours start and stop at the same timeNo double entries; working-time rules evaluated once per change
Searches while others change dataResults respect permissions at every moment; no errors; latency within budget

The load run and the invariants test run against both SQLite and PostgreSQL; the browser scenarios of ten Playwright contexts run on SQLite only, because each worker of the end-to-end tests starts its own server on its own data folder (ADR-0023) and a PostgreSQL database for each of them is not worth what it would add: the behaviour that differs between the databases (the conditional writes of the locks, the order of events) is what the load run and the invariants test cover on both. The short version (2 minutes) runs in CI; the long version (30 minutes, mixed workload) runs nightly and checks invariants afterwards: every change has an event, no lock outlives its lease, no text is lost.

The two ways to run them

  • Ten browsers (web/app/e2e/concurrent/): each person has a browser context of their own, signed in through the API (the sign-in has its own tests). The tests read what the people see (Saved, the "… is editing" note, Edit anyway, the conflict note with Use mine, Compare and save), never only timing, and wait for the answer of the server or for a note on the screen, not for a fixed time. The scenarios of the table above are iss_17_three_people_edit_one_description_and_the_first_text_is_kept, iss_17_a_lock_holders_network_drops_and_the_text_comes_back_with_compare_and_save, iss_17_two_people_change_one_status_within_a_second_and_one_of_them_is_told, iss_17_ten_people_change_ten_fields_of_one_issue_and_every_change_lands_once, iss_09_changing_many_issues_skips_the_one_changed_since_the_preview_and_names_it, which previews a change of status for four issues, lets one editor save the text of one of them, confirms the change and reads on the screen of the person that the issue is named and left alone while the others changed with one event each, and iss_09_changing_many_issues_changes_the_one_somebody_is_editing_and_their_text_is_saved_after, which previews the same kind of change, lets Ben hold the lock of the description with text that is not saved, confirms the change (all four issues change, Ben's too) and has Ben save: his text lands without Compare and save, and his issue has one status event and one text event (the preview and the change are previewBulkChange and applyBulkChange; web/app/e2e/support/bulk.ts is the one place that knows their bodies). The scenario of the dropped network says which console lines it expects (tolerate) from the browser of the holder, and only while that browser is offline; every other console error, every uncaught error and every other browser stays checked. tolerate( may only be used in concurrent/locks.spec.ts (TEST-CONCURRENT). The lock must free within the lease (60 seconds), plus the few seconds the page takes to look again; the time the test waits is made from leaseSeconds and heartbeatSeconds of the generated constants, never from a number of its own. The lock scenarios also run in the WebKit phone project.
  • cargo xtask load --people 10 [--minutes N | --nightly] [--database sqlite|postgres] (xtask/src/load/): the API at speed. xtask builds the program, starts the database of the run (the throwaway PostgreSQL for the second run) and runs the Node driver web/tooling/load/main.ts, which starts a server on the port loadTestServer and a data folder that xtask gave it, makes an organization (one project, six shared issues, Team members), lets the people change titles, edit descriptions under their locks (some editors vanish without letting go, some take the editing over), write comments and read, and writes what each person kept, was refused and read to a book (a JSON file). When the server has stopped, xtask runs bb-load-check on the book and the database of the run, which judges the invariants of the next section. The driver defines no invariant. Without --database it runs on both databases; tools/dev/load.json holds the defaults (ten people, two minutes, thirty for --nightly) and the name of the variable that carries the database address. cargo xtask ci runs it.
  • Against the database (test_concurrent_invariants_hold_after_a_run in bb-server, both databases in cargo test under cargo xtask db run): ten people change four issues together over HTTP while the clock of the test runs on until the last person is done, so leases really run out (a person who types for longer than the lease waits for the clock, not for real time), and then the invariants are read from the database by the same function the load run ends in.

Invariants after every run

They are written once, as the function check of the crate bb-load-check (judge.rs): the test of the server builds its book in memory and calls it, cargo xtask load calls it through the program bb-load-check with the book of the driver. Nothing else defines them (SSOT).

  1. Every change has an event: the events about each issue count each version from 2 up to its version once, one event for each change that was kept (events about a lock taken over or let go count no version), and there is one event for each comment.
  2. Versions only go up, one at a time: the versions of the kept changes of an issue are 2 up to its version, each once, and what one person reads of an issue never goes down.
  3. No lock outlives its lease: no lock row ends later than the lease (60 seconds) from now, nobody holds a lock when the leases are over (in a load run nobody starts to edit under a lock in the last 70 seconds), and after the purge no row of a lock is left. One definition, used while the people work (the test of the server) and at the end (both).
  4. No text is lost: a save that was refused (lock lost, taken over, text changed) is the draft of the person at once, the heartbeat draft of an editor who vanished is still there after the lease, and the description is the text of the last save that was kept.

Enforced by: TEST-CONCURRENT (the scenarios, the invariants test and the load step of cargo xtask ci are there and not switched off), TEST-EDIT-LOCKS (the browser scenarios of the locks).

Local ports (ADR-0023)

Your machine runs other Vite projects, so Bugaboo never uses default ports. All ports live in tools/dev/ports.json (single source); Vite, Playwright, the server and xtask read them from there, and every tool uses strictPort, so a busy port fails with a clear message instead of silently moving.

OffsetUsed by
0Bugaboo server in development (API + embedded app)
1Vite dev server (hot reload)
2Vite preview of a production build
3Server instance for end-to-end tests (fresh sample database)
4Vitest UI
10–29Parallel Playwright workers, one server and database each
30Load-test server
40Throwaway PostgreSQL for tests (cargo xtask db start)

The offsets are inside a block of 100 ports. Each work folder bugaboo.winN has its own block, starting at 47200 + (N − 1) · 100 (win1 47200–47299, win3 47400–47499, up to win9 48000–48099), so folders that build and test at the same time never share a port; any other folder uses block 1 and BUGABOO_PORT_BLOCK names another one. The table above shows block 1: the server of the first folder is on 47200, of the third on 47400.

The installed product asks for its port in the setup wizard (suggesting 8443 and checking that it's free); these development ports never appear in a customer installation.

Security: threat model and personal-data flows

Part of the security and data-flow documentation (COMP-07) for the CRA technical file and for customers' own risk assessments. It covers what is built so far and grows with every milestone: each milestone review checks that new entry points appear here.

The method is STRIDE per trust boundary (boundaries from Context). Every threat names the mitigation and what proves it: a check from the catalogue (tools/checks/catalog.toml), a test, or review when a person decides.

Scope (status: M3 planned)

In scope nowComes later (own section then)
HTTPS and start-up config, security headers, sign-in (password, passkey, two-step codes), sessions, invitations, first-run setup code, rate limits, the security log, stored secrets, logs (M1); the permission engine (roles, groups, assignments, No access, field masks, Who sees people), projects and short names, access keys, two-step sign-in by role, settings in layers (M2)Issues (M3), attachments and mail (M4), search language (M5), MCP and the assistant (M8), Remove a person and exports (M9), webhooks (M12), the served model's control plane (M14)

Attack surface

flowchart LR
  browser(["Browser<br/>(untrusted)"])
  console(["Server console<br/>(operator)"])
  subgraph server["bugaboo process"]
    tls["HTTPS<br/>rustls"]
    hdr["Security headers<br/>rate limits"]
    api["/api/v1<br/>problem+json"]
    auth["Sign-in<br/>sessions, CSRF"]
    store["bb-store"]
  end
  subgraph data["Data folder (owner-only)"]
    db[("database")]
    keys["keys/master.key"]
    cert["tls/"]
    logs["logs"]
  end
  browser -- "1 · HTTPS" --> tls --> hdr --> api --> auth --> store --> db
  console -- "setup code<br/>bugaboo setup" --> server
  store --> keys
  tls --> cert
  server --> logs

Entry points in M1: the HTTPS listener (pages, assets, /api/v1, /health/*), the console and bugaboo.toml, and the data folder on disk. M2 adds no new listener: the new routes are below /api/v1, and scripts reach them with an access key (Authorization: Bearer bb_…) instead of a cookie. The sample-organization program (bb-sample) is a developer tool and is not shipped before OPS-12.

Permissions, projects and access keys (M2)

The model is ADR-0025 and §7, Authorization model. The trust boundary is the same (browser or script ↔ server); what is new is that the server now decides between people who are all signed in. The packages that build a row add its test when they merge; a name in the last column that does not exist yet is the test the package's plan asks for.

M2 adds where people work (groups and roles), projects, access keys and each person's own settings. The marks below are decided here (ADR-0025); each package writes them on its entities, and cargo xtask gen privacy then lists them on the generated page docs/privacy/personal-data.md. Enforced by: DATA-MARKS.

A new category, organization: where a person works, meaning their groups and the roles they have, and where. Decision records

Each record explains one decision: the situation, what we decided, what follows from it, what else we considered, and which checks enforce it.

ADR-0001: Modular monolith in one binary

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

Bugaboo must be secure, fast and installable on Windows, Linux and WSL by people without operations experience. The scale target (500 people, 1 M issues) fits one machine.

Decision

Build one Rust binary containing the API, the embedded browser app, background jobs and the MCP server. Inside, use a hexagonal structure: a pure domain core (bb-core, bb-policy, bb-searchlang, bb-markdown), use cases (bb-app) that depend only on ports (traits), and adapters (bb-store, bb-files, bb-ai, bb-notify, bb-api, bb-mcp). Module boundaries are crates, and dependency rules are checked by cargo xtask check only ARCH-DEPS.

Consequences

  • One process, one security boundary, one thing to install, back up and update.
  • Use cases are testable with in-memory fakes; adapters are tested separately.
  • Scaling beyond one machine would need work later (accepted: not a 1.0 goal).

Alternatives considered

  • Microservices: more moving parts, more attack surface, harder installation. Rejected.
  • One big crate: faster to start, but boundaries erode and compile times grow. Rejected.

Enforced by

ARCH-DEPS, ARCH-HTTP-EDGE, ARCH-MAP-SYNC, META-NEW-MODULE (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0002: HTTP stack: Tokio, axum, rustls

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

We need a mature async HTTP server with good middleware, HTTPS without system OpenSSL, and easy static builds for Windows and Linux.

Decision

Use tokio as the runtime, axum for routing and extractors, tower-http for compression, headers and limits, and rustls (with tokio-rustls) for TLS, using the ring crypto provider so static musl and Windows builds need no C toolchain beyond what Rust ships. instant-acme handles certificates from ACME.

Consequences

  • No OpenSSL dependency; memory-safe TLS.
  • axum extractors give one place to turn credentials into an actor.

Alternatives considered

  • actix-web: fine, but a smaller middleware ecosystem around tower.
  • aws-lc-rs provider: stronger FIPS story, but needs CMake/C for static builds; revisit if FIPS is ever required.

Enforced by

SEC-HEADERS, DEP-LICENSES (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0003: Databases: SQLite by default, PostgreSQL optional

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

Installation must work with zero setup, but larger installations and the served model need a server database.

Decision

Support SQLite (bundled, WAL mode) and PostgreSQL 16+ through sqlx. Write queries with sea-query (bound through sea-query-sqlx) so one query definition produces both dialects. Define the schema and migrations once in Rust with the same query builder; both databases run the same migration list. Dialect-specific code is allowed only behind the bb-store port implementations and needs a comment explaining why.

Consequences

  • Every repository test runs against both databases in CI.
  • Some PostgreSQL features (for example row-level security) are not used in core paths; authorization stays in bb-policy anyway.
  • The served model uses PostgreSQL; self-hosted installations start with SQLite and can migrate with bugaboo migrate-to-postgres.

Alternatives considered

  • PostgreSQL only: simpler code, harder installation. Rejected for the default.
  • SeaORM: less control over generated SQL for permission predicates. Rejected.
  • Two hand-written migration folders: violates SSOT. Rejected.

Enforced by

ARCH-SQL-EDGE, DATA-MIGRATIONS, ARCH-DB-PARITY (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0004: Authorization: one policy engine and Authorized

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04 · refined by ADR-0025

Context

Security is priority one. Permissions go down to single fields and single issues, and many entry points (UI, API, search, MCP, assistant, e-mail, webhooks, exports, live updates) must all obey them.

Decision

  • All decisions are made by bb-policy: permission catalogue, role assignments on the project tree with inheritance and explicit deny, field masks, visibility groups and token scopes.
  • Data leaves the domain only as Authorized<T>, whose constructor is private to bb-policy. It carries the field mask and applies it when serialized. Returning plain domain types from bb-app is a compile error at the API layer.
  • Searches get the actor's visibility predicates compiled into the same SQL query, and the parser only knows readable fields, so a hidden field looks exactly like an unknown one.
  • Outbound channels (notifications, webhooks, live updates, exports, assistant context) apply the receiver's mask.

Consequences

  • Forgetting a check is hard: the types don't line up.
  • A generated test matrix (roles × permissions × fields × entry points) runs on every build.
  • Per-request caching of evaluations keeps it fast.

Alternatives considered

  • Checks in each handler: easy to forget one. Rejected.
  • Database row-level security: PostgreSQL only, and field-level rules would still be needed in code. Rejected.
  • External policy engines (OPA, Cedar): another language and runtime to secure and ship; our model is fixed and well understood. Rejected for now; the catalogue could be exported to Cedar later.

Enforced by

ARCH-AUTHZ-ONLY, ARCH-API-OUT, ARCH-PERMS, SEC-MATRIX (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0005: Search language: one Rust crate, also in the browser

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

People need simple filter buttons and an advanced typed search, converting exactly into each other, with the same behavior in the browser and on the server, and without copying another vendor's language.

Decision

Write bb-searchlang: lexer, parser, syntax tree, canonical printer, checker and suggestions, with no I/O. Simple search edits the syntax tree; Advanced search edits text that parses into the same tree. Compile the crate to WebAssembly (bb-wasm) for instant highlighting, suggestions and error messages in the browser. The server compiles the tree to SQL in bb-store.

Consequences

  • One grammar (SSOT). Property test: parse(print(tree)) == tree.
  • WebAssembly adds download size; it's loaded only when search is first used, within the WebAssembly budget in tools/checks/perf-bundle.toml, shared with the Markdown renderer.

Alternatives considered

  • A grammar written twice (Rust and TypeScript): drifts. Rejected.
  • Parser generators (pest, lalrpop): fine, but hand-written recursive descent gives better plain-language error messages. Decision left to the milestone, as long as the crate stays I/O-free.

Enforced by

ARCH-PURE, ARCH-WASM, TEST-SEARCH-ROUNDTRIP (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0006: Own fields stored in a typed value table

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

Organizations add their own fields to issues, time entries, work days, documents, releases and projects. They must be filterable, sortable, permissioned per field, and fast on both databases.

Decision

Store values in one field_value table: (entity_kind, entity_id, field_id, value_text, value_number, value_date, value_ref, position), with indexes per typed column and per (field_id, value_*). Multi-value fields use several rows. Field definitions (type, rules, options, look) live in field and field_option.

Consequences

  • The search compiler joins field_value per referenced field; indexes keep it fast at 1 M issues.
  • Built-in fields stay real columns; own fields and built-in fields look the same to search, permissions and the API.

Alternatives considered

  • A JSON column per entity: indexing differs between SQLite and PostgreSQL and is weaker for sorting. Rejected.
  • Adding real columns at runtime: schema changes from the UI are risky and slow. Rejected.

Enforced by

ARCH-DB-PARITY, PERF-BENCH; table shape: review (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0007: Event log and outbox as the single source of change

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

History, notifications, webhooks, the security log, full-text indexing and live updates all need to know what changed. Writing to each separately would duplicate logic and lose consistency.

Decision

Every use case appends domain events (actor, channel, entity, field changes before → after, reason) in the same transaction as the change, plus an outbox row. After commit, consumers (history, notifications, webhooks, security log, search index, live updates) read the outbox, remember their position, and are idempotent.

Consequences

  • One write path; every consumer sees the same facts.
  • The security log is hash-chained from the security-relevant events.
  • Events contain personal data, so they carry personal-data marks and follow keep-and-delete rules (ADR-0015).

Change (2026-10-10, M3 WP-07)

The first consumer of the outbox is the history of an issue (history_entry, ISS-06). It reads events after its stored position and writes one row per event and issue with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, so a repeat changes nothing. The rows commit first and the position moves after them in a second step, so a stop in between makes the next round read the same events again and the repeat is harmless; it resumes after a restart. The rows hold the facts; the reader's field mask is applied when the history is read, never when it is built, so a change of roles changes what is shown at once. The consumer runs when a history is read and as the daily job history.catch-up of the job runner (ADR-0017), which is also queued at every server start (M3-F71).

Alternatives considered

  • Full event sourcing: more power than needed and harder for agents to get right. Rejected; current state stays in normal tables.
  • Database triggers: dialect-specific and invisible in code. Rejected.

Enforced by

ARCH-EVENTS (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).
