ADR-0008: API first: OpenAPI from Rust, TypeScript client generated

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

The browser app must be a normal API client (principle 3), and API types must exist once (ODR).

Decision

Describe every endpoint and type in Rust with utoipa; generate the OpenAPI 3.1 document at build time; generate the TypeScript types and a thin fetch client with openapi-typescript into web/packages/api-client. Error codes, permission names and validation schemas are part of the document. The CI check generated-code-freshness fails if the client is out of date.

Consequences

  • The browser can't call what the API doesn't offer; third parties get the same API.
  • API versioning: /api/v1/…; breaking changes need a new version and an ADR.

Alternatives considered

  • Hand-written TypeScript types: drift. Rejected.
  • GraphQL: flexible, but per-field authorization and query-cost control are harder to make airtight. Rejected; ?fields= gives lean responses.

Enforced by

DOC-GENERATED, ARCH-WEB-API, ARCH-LEAN, ARCH-VERSIONED (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0009: Browser app: React 19, Vite, TanStack, React Aria

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

The UI must be slick, accessible (WCAG 2.2 AA), fast on phones, and buildable by agents with clear patterns.

Decision

  • React 19 with function components and hooks; Vite for building and splitting.
  • TanStack Router for type-safe routes and typed URL search parameters (searches and presentations live in the URL).
  • TanStack Query as the only store for server data; TanStack Virtual for long lists.
  • React Aria Components as the base of every interactive component (focus, keyboard, screen readers, touch).
  • Tiptap (ProseMirror) for the document editor; d3-force for the relation map layout; timeline, calendar and charts are our own components on shared primitives.

Consequences

  • No global client state library: URL + query cache + local component state cover the needs.
  • Heavy features are lazy-loaded to meet the 250 KB initial budget, and so are their texts: each feature brings its own part of the message catalog (ADR-0028).

Alternatives considered

  • Next.js / server rendering: adds a Node server to install and complicates the CSP. Rejected.
  • Headless UI kits without accessibility depth: more work to reach WCAG. Rejected.

Enforced by

ARCH-WEB-FEATURES, PERF-BUNDLE, TEST-A11Y, LINT-TS (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0010: Styling through design tokens only

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04 · the styling decisions (the token file, the generator, CSS Modules) are replaced by ADR-0026; the rest stands

Context

Four built-in themes, a theme editor, custom field looks and strict CSP, all without letting customization inject code.

Decision

  • design/tokens.json (W3C Design Tokens format) is the only source of colors, fonts, sizes, radii and shadows, for all four themes. Replaced by ADR-0026: design/theme.kdl is the only source of every value and every component rule.
  • cargo xtask gen tokens produces: CSS variables per theme, TypeScript token names, and the Rust validation used by the theme editor (allowed values, contrast checks). Replaced by ADR-0026: cargo xtask gen theme writes the one style sheet, the TypeScript names and the Rust theme choices.
  • Components use CSS Modules with var(--token) only. The hooks reject raw colors, pixel sizes outside tokens and inline styles. Replaced by ADR-0026: components carry no class names and no styles; they emit data-part, data-variant and data-state, and the rules in the theme file use tokens only.
  • Custom themes and field looks store token values or token names, never CSS.
  • The choices of a person that are not a theme (Compact spacing, Larger text, Less motion) are variants in the token file: each switches token values through an attribute on the page (data-spacing, data-text, data-motion), and Less motion also follows the device. Sizes of spacing and text are written as the usual size times a factor token, so one choice scales everything. Where the layout changes (bp-tablet, bp-computer) is a token too, read by the app through the generated TypeScript.
  • Every theme has stronger colors for prefers-contrast: more (contrastMore). STY-CONTRAST checks them at 7:1 for text and 3:1 for lines.

Consequences

  • The design pages in docs/design/ use the generated CSS (theme.css, the tokens without the component rules).

Alternatives considered

  • Tailwind CSS: harder to enforce "tokens only"; class soup in agent-written code. Rejected.
  • CSS-in-JS at runtime: costs performance and needs CSP exceptions. Rejected.

Enforced by

STY-TOKENS, LINT-CSS, STY-CONTRAST (see tools/checks/catalog.toml); for the styling decisions that ADR-0026 replaced, THEME-ONLY too.

ADR-0011: One Markdown renderer for server and browser

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04 · changed 2026-10-09 (M3 WP-02: the writer replaces ammonia, see "Change")

Context

Issue descriptions, comments and documents are Markdown written by people, so they're untrusted. The preview must match what others will see.

Decision

bb-markdown uses pulldown-cmark to parse and writes the HTML itself from the parser's events, with one allow list: only the tags and attributes of its writer can be in the output, raw HTML in the text is turned into text, links get rel="noopener noreferrer" and open outside, only http, https, mailto and our own pages are links, and images come from our own origin or from a host an admin allows. Issue IDs and mentions come back as tokens (resolved later with permission checks), shown as chips. The same crate runs on the server and, via WebAssembly, in the browser for previews.

Consequences

  • One allow list (SSOT), in the writer; no client-side HTML rendering library.
  • Nothing is parsed back and cleaned, so there is no gap between what the writer meant and what a sanitizer's HTML parser reads (mutation XSS has no place to start).
  • The WebAssembly module stays small: the budget of the module is in tools/checks/perf-bundle.toml (architecture §8, PERF-04), and the search language shares it.
  • The browser shows the HTML with one Trusted Types policy, bugaboo-markdown, in the one component MarkdownView (SEC-RICHTEXT).
  • The document editor (Tiptap) stores Markdown; its schema is limited to what bb-markdown renders.

Change (2026-10-09, M3 WP-02)

The first plan was to sanitize with ammonia after pulldown-cmark's own HTML. Measured on the real module: ammonia brings an HTML parser (html5ever), the URL library with its tables for international domain names, and their data, about 250 KB more with Brotli, so the module would be about four times the size of the parser alone, far over its budget, which the search language (M5) has to share. Writing the HTML from the events needs none of that, is easier to read as one allow list, and keeps the security property: the output holds only what the writer can write. The corpus test (SEC-13) and the property tests check the output for tags, attributes and addresses that the allow list does not have.

Change (2026-10-10, M3 WP-07)

A comment is shown to many readers, and what a token may become depends on the reader: an issue ID is a chip only for a reader who may see that issue, a mention only if the writer may name that person. The renderer stays pure and knows nothing of this. Options.plain_tokens lists the places (in Rendered::tokens) that stay plain text; the server renders once to find the tokens, decides, and renders again with the list. The places do not move, so the decision is made on the same list both times. The rendering is per reader and never stored.

Alternatives considered

  • marked/markdown-it + DOMPurify in the browser: a second renderer that could disagree with the server. Rejected.
  • pulldown-cmark + ammonia (the first plan): a clean-up after the HTML is made; too big for WebAssembly (see "Change"). Rejected for the browser module, and one renderer must serve both.

Enforced by

ARCH-PURE, ARCH-WASM, SEC-PATTERNS, SEC-RICHTEXT, PERF-BUNDLE (the budget of the module) (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0012: One binary for sold and served

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

Bugaboo may be sold (self-hosted) or served (hosted by us); the business model isn't decided.

Decision

  • The same signed binary runs in both models (DIST-01).
  • Served = one isolated instance per customer (own database, file store, encryption key and address) in the EU, plus a separate control plane for set-up, updates, backups and health (DIST-02). The control plane uses an operator API that cannot read customer data; emergency access needs the customer's approval and is logged in their security log (DIST-03).
  • Sold: a signed offline license file; no phone-home and no telemetry (DIST-04).
  • Export and import work between the two, both ways (DIST-06).

Consequences

  • "One organization per installation" stays true in both models; no tenant column in every table.
  • Hosting cost per customer is higher than a shared multi-tenant system; accepted for isolation and simplicity.

Alternatives considered

  • Multi-tenant shared database: cheaper to host, but every query needs a tenant filter and one bug can leak across customers. Rejected for 1.0.

Enforced by

review (deployment design; tested end to end in the served-model milestone), DEP-LICENSES for the license file tooling (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0013: AI: one provider interface, one tool registry, no decisions about people

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

AI is priority three, but must never bypass permissions, must resist prompt injection, and must stay outside the AI Act's high-risk and banned uses.

Decision

  • One provider trait with adapters for Anthropic (default) and OpenAI-compatible endpoints (covers local models).
  • One tool registry used by both the assistant and MCP. Each tool calls a bb-app use case as the actor.
  • Assistant writes are proposals; nothing changes until the person clicks Apply.
  • Context builder sends only readable, non-excluded fields and fences people's text as untrusted.
  • Designed out: tools that rank, evaluate or assign people, read working hours, or analyse mood. They don't exist in the registry.
  • AI output saved into issues or documents is marked Written with the assistant.

Consequences

  • MCP and the assistant can't drift apart in rules or capabilities.
  • Adding a tool needs a review against the AI Act rules (checklist in the ADR template).

Alternatives considered

  • Separate tool code for MCP and the assistant: duplicates permission handling. Rejected.
  • Letting the assistant act directly: prompt-injection risk. Rejected.

Enforced by

ARCH-AI-TOOLS, ARCH-PERMS, SEC-MATRIX (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0014: One check runner for hooks, agents and CI

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

Checks (formatting, linting, hard-coded text, tokens only, terminology, licenses, register, architecture docs, personal-data marks, size budgets) must behave the same on Windows, Linux and WSL, for people, AI agents and CI.

Decision

  • cargo xtask is the single entry point: cargo xtask check staged, check all, gen …, release …. It's Rust, so it runs wherever the code builds.
  • lefthook runs check staged on commit, check push on push and the commit-message check; cargo xtask setup installs it and the hooks.
  • Claude Code hooks (.claude/settings.json) run the relevant checks after each file edit, so agents get immediate feedback.
  • CI runs check all plus slow checks (benchmarks, end-to-end, SBOM).
  • Rust: rustfmt formats, clippy lints (warnings are errors, selected pedantic lints on).
  • TypeScript 7: oxfmt formats; oxlint lints, with oxlint-tsgolint for type-aware rules. tsgolint is built on typescript-go, the TypeScript 7 compiler itself, so it understands TypeScript 7 exactly. tsc (TypeScript 7) does the type check.
  • CSS: stylelint enforces "tokens only"; formatting by oxfmt (or Biome, if oxfmt doesn't cover CSS at setup time).
  • Other files: taplo (TOML), rumdl (Markdown), typos (spelling), lychee (links), actionlint (CI files).
  • Pattern rules across Rust and TypeScript (no literal UI text, no raw colors, no unwrap in production code, no SQL built with format!, Authorized<T> only in bb-policy) are ast-grep rules in tools/rules/.
  • Every check is listed once in tools/checks/catalog.toml (ADR-0020).

Consequences

  • One list of checks (SSOT), visible in xtask/src/checks/.

Alternatives considered

  • Shell scripts: differ between Windows and Linux. Rejected.
  • ESLint + typescript-eslint: typescript-eslint supports TypeScript only up to 6.0. Rejected.
  • Biome: a good all-in-one tool, but its type-aware rules use its own inference instead of the TypeScript 7 compiler. Kept as fallback for formatting.

Enforced by

META-WIRING, META-CATALOG, META-SPEED, FMT-, LINT- (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0015: Personal-data marks drive GDPR features

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

GDPR features (export, removal, keep-and-delete rules, record of processing) break silently when a new feature adds personal data and forgets them.

Decision

Every stored field is marked in its entity definition with a derive attribute, for example #[personal(category = "employee_time", basis = "legal_obligation")] or #[not_personal]. Unmarked fields fail the build. A generated personal-data map drives Download my data, the Remove a person plan, keep-and-delete jobs, the record of processing (Art. 30) and the data-flow map.

Consequences

  • GDPR compliance becomes part of the type system and CI, not a checklist.
  • Events and logs follow the same marks.

Alternatives considered

  • A hand-maintained spreadsheet of personal data: drifts. Rejected.

Enforced by

DATA-MARKS, DATA-LOGS (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

Amendment (M1)

  • A person's ID is itself personal data: a pseudonym, marked #[personal(category = "identity", basis = "legitimate_interests")]. After Remove a person it is kept only as the link to the Former user … tombstone.
  • #[not_personal] is accepted only for field types that cannot hold personal data (they implement NotPersonal: numbers, moments, IDs of records, the words of the marks, and types that say so). Free text is never on that list. Remaining limits are written on the generated page docs/privacy/personal-data.md.
  • Checked by DATA-MARKS and by the compile-fail tests in crates/bb-core/tests/compile_fail.rs (not_personal_person, not_personal_text).

ADR-0016: Full-text search inside the database

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

Text search must respect permissions and work on both databases at the scale target.

Decision

Use SQLite FTS5 and PostgreSQL text search (tsvector with GIN index) behind one port. The search compiler adds the text condition to the same SQL query as the permission predicates. Index updates come from the outbox.

Consequences

  • No second index to secure, back up or rebuild separately.
  • Ranking quality is good, not perfect; acceptable for 1.0.

Alternatives considered

  • tantivy or an external search server: better ranking, but permission filtering outside SQL and another store to protect. Rejected for 1.0.

Enforced by

SEC-MATRIX (search entry point), ARCH-DB-PARITY (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0017: Background jobs stored in the database

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

Previews, virus scans, e-mail, webhooks, digests, backups, keep-and-delete runs and person removal need reliable background work.

Decision

A small job queue in the database (job table with run_at, attempts, lease) run by bb-jobs inside the server process. Leases use SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED on PostgreSQL and the single writer queue on SQLite. Schedules (cron-like) are settings in the registry.

Consequences

  • Nothing extra to install; jobs survive restarts.
  • Throughput is enough for the scale target; heavy work (previews) is limited by a worker pool size setting.

Alternatives considered

  • Redis/RabbitMQ: more installation and attack surface. Rejected.

Enforced by

review; every job type has an idempotency test (part of ARCH-EVENTS test harness) (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

Amendment (M3 WP-08)

  • The runner exists (bb-jobs). It depends on bb-app only (ARCH-DEPS): spawn(services, every) calls Ctx::run_due_jobs() on a timer, and bb-server starts it. The queue is behind the port JobStore; a round takes up to five due jobs under a lease of 120 seconds, runs each, reports it done (it leaves the queue) or failed, and a job that did a step queues the next one when more is left. A job that failed five starts goes to the dead-letter list.
  • Kinds so far: bulk.step (changing many issues: 100 issues in a step, progress kept in the table bulk_run after each issue, so a step that stops half way goes on at the next issue and no issue is changed twice) and issues.renew-ids (ADR-0021). bulk.step judges again at run time what it does to each issue, with the permissions of the person who asked (Ctx::acting, ctx_acting_as). issues.renew-ids judges nothing: it finishes a change that was judged when the person changed the mode of IDs (they needed the right to change the project's settings then), so it renews the IDs of every issue of the project that does not have the new mode yet, and names that person on the events. Both are idempotent.
  • When a change is a job: more than 1,000 issues (BULK_JOB_ABOVE); an access key may not start one (auth.access_key_not_allowed, M3-F121).
  • Jobs that come back every day. editing.purge_drafts (drafts, notes for people who were editing and lock rows that ran out) and history.catch-up (the history reads the events, ADR-0007) are daily kinds; there is no timer of the server any more (M3-F30, M3-F71). bb-server calls Ctx::start_daily_jobs when it starts, which queues a round of each at once, and every round queues the next one a day later before it does its work, so a round that fails (the queue tries it again) or a worker that stops does not end the days. A round queues the next only when none for a later time waits (JobStore::later_job_waits), so a server that starts twice in a day leaves one chain of rounds, not two. Both are idempotent, and a read of a history still catches up first.
  • Permissions are cached for one step. A step of bulk.step judges its (up to 100) issues with one context, which keeps what the policy engine decided for the person for the whole step (ADR-0025, decision 3: the cache lives as long as its context). A person who loses access while a run goes on is therefore stopped at the next step, not at the next issue: the next step builds a new context and judges from the roles they hold then, and the issues it leaves alone are named with not-found or not-allowed.
  • A stopped worker and the count. The change to an issue and the saving of the progress of the run are two writes. The event of every change a run makes carries a reason that names the run and the item (BulkRun::item_reason); a step that begins at an item whose event is there already (BulkStore::event_with_reason, looked up by the range of event IDs since the run began) counts the issue as changed and goes on, instead of judging it again and reporting that it changed after the preview.
  • A tag or label counts the version. Putting a tag or a label on an issue or taking one off counts the version of the issue up in the same change (by one, whatever the version stored then is: the routes do not take a version, so two people who add or take off different ones both succeed, and so does a tag put on while somebody saves the title; the event carries the version the row has after the count-up. The other way round, a save that read the version before the tag was put on is told that the version changed, like after any other change. An issue that went to the trash in between is not found), so a preview that read the version before sees that the issue changed in between and names it, also in a Pick one group where the label it would replace is not the one the issue has now.
  • One project event for the renewal. ChangeStore::record_changes writes a change with any number of events of its own, also none. A step of issues.renew-ids writes the events of the issues it renews; the step that renews the last also writes the one event of the project (issue-ids).

ADR-0018: One settings registry drives storage, API and dialogs

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

"Everything configurable in the UI" means hundreds of settings across organization, project and person levels. Hand-building each dialog violates DRY and drifts.

Decision

Define each setting once with the settings! macro, which is used only in the registry file of bb-core: key, type, default, allowed levels (organization / project / person), who may change it, help-text message key, and whether admins can lock it. The registry generates storage access, API endpoints, OpenAPI schema and the metadata the UI uses to render settings dialogs (grouped by topic, with search).

Consequences

  • A new setting appears in the right dialog automatically, with its explanation.
  • Special editors (workflow, layout, theme, permissions matrix) are still custom UI, but store their results through the same registry.

Update 2026-10-06 (M2 WP-07, settings in layers)

  • The registry also holds the name of each setting (a message key, next to the explanation), a format for text values (one of a fixed list with the words for each choice, a time zone, the address of a page of the app, the keys of shortcuts) and its levels. One check of a value is used by the store and the use cases.
  • Layers: default, organization, the nearest project up the tree, person; a value the organization locked wins and lower layers are refused. Reset to default takes away the value of one layer. A person's own values are stored in their own table so the person is a column with a personal-data mark.
  • One set of routes and one generic form serve every setting; special editors (the themes with their samples, the keys of shortcuts, the start page) draw their own control and store through the same routes.
  • appearance.theme was replaced by appearance.mode, appearance.light-theme and appearance.dark-theme; migration m0004 carries the stored values over.
  • The settings that exist only for tests (feature test-settings of bb-core) are the way the project level is tested while no real setting is set on a project.

Alternatives considered

  • Hand-written forms per setting: slow and inconsistent. Rejected.

Enforced by

ARCH-SETTINGS (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0019: Edit locks and confirmed saves

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

Bugaboo has no real-time co-editing in 1.0. Without care, two people editing a long description, a comment or a document page overwrite each other, and a save that looks done can silently fail. The UI should feel instant (optimistic), but nobody may lose text.

Decision

Two mechanisms, one for each kind of value:

  1. Short values (status, priority, people, dates, choices): no lock. The change shows at once and is sent with the entity's version (in the body, see the amendment). A stale version gets a conflict answer.
  2. Long text (descriptions, long-text own fields, a comment being edited, document pages, and admin editors such as workflows, layouts and themes): an edit lock.
    • Taken on the first keystroke, not on opening, so readers never block anyone.
    • A lease, not a permanent lock: stored in the database (edit_lock: what, who, session, token, expires at). It lasts 60 s and is renewed by a heartbeat every 15 s while the editor is open. Closing the tab, losing the network or a crash simply lets it run out.
    • Others see "Ana is editing the description" and the field is read-only for them. They can Ask Ana to finish (a notification) or, with permission, Edit anyway: the lock moves to them, Ana is told, and Ana's unsaved text is kept as her draft.
    • Drafts are saved privately on the server every few seconds and in the browser (IndexedDB), so a crash, reload or lost lock never loses text.
    • Saving sends the text with the lock token and the base version. The server rejects a save without a valid token (lock lost or taken over) or with a stale version.
    • Admins can release a stuck lock; it's recorded in the security log.

Confirmed saves (both kinds):

  • The screen shows the change immediately and marks it Saving….
  • The server's answer confirms it (Saved), or the UI explains exactly what happened and keeps the person's text:
    • conflict — "Ben changed this a moment ago. [Compare]";
    • lock lost or taken over — "Your editing time ran out / Ben took over. Your text is kept. [Compare and save]";
    • offline — "Not saved yet. We'll try again when you're back online." Pending saves survive a reload.
  • Watching open items: until live updates exist (ISS-14), the browser checks the versions of what's on screen every 30 s and on focus (one small request). If someone changed something you just saved, you see "Ben changed the description after you. [Show changes]".

Consequences

  • Nobody loses text silently; every failure has a plain explanation and a way forward.
  • Locks need no live-update channel; plain HTTP heartbeats work everywhere.
  • Lock records hold person IDs; they are deleted when they expire (no keep period).

Alternatives considered

  • Real-time co-editing (CRDT, Yjs): much more complex; planned for later (DOC-10).
  • Locks taken when opening: block people who only read. Rejected.
  • In-memory locks: lost on restart and invisible to admins. Rejected; the database is cheap enough.

Enforced by

ARCH-VERSIONED, TEST-EDIT-LOCKS (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

Amendment (M3, 2026-10-09)

  • The version travels in the body. Every change sends the version it read as version in the request body, as the M2 routes already do, not in If-Match; a change of many issues carries one version per issue, which a header cannot. ARCH-VERSIONED reads the body of every change operation in the API description; a route without a version (signing in, making a new record) is named with its reason in an exemption file.
  • The conflict answer is structured. edit.version_changed (409) holds who changed it (a PersonRef for the reader), when, which fields, and the current values the reader may see; the browser writes the sentence from it with the reader's field mask and Who sees people, so an error message keeps no placeholder (architecture §7, Errors). For short values the sentence is "Ben changed Priority to Critical 2 minutes ago." with Keep Ben's and Use mine (decision M3-Q5); for long text it stays Compare and save.
  • Drafts are saved with the heartbeat (every 15 s) and kept until the text is saved or thrown away, at most 30 days after their last change (decision M3-Q9); a draft for a new issue belongs to the person, the project and the form. A job deletes the old ones (ADR-0017).
  • Ask … to finish and Edit anyway reach the person who is editing at their next heartbeat, in the open page; e-mail and in-app notifications add the same in M4 (decision M3-Q3).

Amendment (M3 WP-04)

  • Numbers. The lease (60 s), the heartbeat (15 s), the keep period of a draft (30 days) and the most records one check of versions takes (50) are named constants in bb-core::edit; the browser client reads them from the generated editing.generated.ts.
  • Any record. A lock and a draft are about one part of a record named by its EntityRef. A kind of record says where it sits, which version it has and what a person needs to change it (EditableRecords); the editing code names no kind. Routes whose permission depends on the kind declare by-record; Edit anyway and the release of a stuck lock declare the permission edit-anyway; Edit anyway also needs the right to change the record (a lock that could not be kept is not taken), the release of a stuck lock does not (an administrator ends it, whatever the record).
  • Events. The lease, the heartbeat and the draft write no domain event (they are the state of an open editor); Edit anyway, Ask … to finish and an administrator's release write one, and the release also writes edit_lock.released into the security log, but only when it ended the lease of another person that was still running; that person finds a note at their next heartbeat saying who released it.
  • What a lock stores. The person who holds it and the editor (tab) ID, not a session. The token is only half the proof: the heartbeat, the release and the save also compare the holder with the person who asks, so a token that leaks to another signed-in person opens nothing. Nobody renews a lock after its holder signs out, so the lease ends within a minute (60 s) after.
  • An event that counts the version up holds the change version. The conflict answer is made from the newest event about the record that holds it, never from the newest event of any kind (ask-to-finish, release and group member events do not count). A person's value in such an event is never stored as a raw ID where the conflict can return it. Each kind of record says which of its changes a conflict may show and which hold a person (EditableRecords::shows); a name nobody listed stays hidden. The sign-up policy, which sets two settings together, is one record with a version of its own, kept in its own table (policy_version) where no change or reset of a setting can touch it; it has one route, and the generic settings routes refuse and do not list its two settings (changed_only_on_its_own_screen). The conflict finds the newest event that counted the version up through all the events of the record, a page at a time, so no window cuts it short. The names of the members of an event are defined once (bb-app member::), for the writer and for the list of what a conflict may show; the stored words did not change. A version counts up in one place (bb_core::version::next).
  • Housekeeping. The daily job editing.purge_drafts of the job runner (ADR-0017) runs purge_drafts (drafts, old notes, lock rows that ran out); it is also queued at every server start (M3-F30).
  • Locks and drafts belong to a tab of a signed-in person. Every lock and draft route needs the session of a browser (ctx.session_actor), so an access key is turned away from them, whatever it may change elsewhere.
  • Nothing typed is dropped. The heartbeat keeps the text so far as the person's draft even when the lock is gone; a save that is refused (edit.lock_lost, edit.taken_over, edit.version_changed) keeps its text as the draft. The notes for the person who was editing are handed over once at their next heartbeat.
  • Enforced by: ARCH-VERSIONED (every change takes a version, or is named in tools/checks/version-exemptions.toml; a save of long text also takes lock_token; both are required in the body), TEST-EDIT-LOCKS (server part, both databases; the browser scenarios of WP-10 are in web/app/e2e/concurrent/).

Amendment (M3 WP-05)

  • A long-text own field is saved only under the lock. PUT /api/v1/issues/{issue}/fields/{field}/text is the one route that changes it (saveIssueFieldText, in LONG_TEXT_ROUTES); PATCH of an issue and of a project refuse such a field. A refused save, also one refused before it is tried (a rule, a stale version), keeps the text as the person's draft.
  • A new issue may be made with a long text, like the description. POST /issues takes long-text own fields, because nothing is edited yet and no lock can exist; every later change goes through the lock.
  • A long-text field can only be made for issues. Projects have no lock route for it yet (M3-F49); the server refuses the pair when the field is made.

Amendment (M3 WP-06)

  • The issue is known to the editing code. bb-app knows the issue like it knows projects, roles and groups, so locks, drafts and the check of versions work on it without EditableRecords: issues/editing.rs gives the place, the version and the permission to change (Change issues, or Change own issues for the person who reported it), and editing/conflict.rs says which of its changes a conflict may show. EditableRecords stays for kinds the program adds from outside (the notes of the tests). A new kind that bb-app itself owns is added the same way, in these two places.
  • The description is saved by its own route. PUT /issues/{issue}/description takes text, version and lock_token and saves through Ctx::save_text (ARCH-EVENTS accepts that call as the other way a command writes its event). It is listed in LONG_TEXT_ROUTES, so ARCH-VERSIONED holds it to the token.
  • The server renders what the page shows. The answer of getIssue holds description_html, made by bb-markdown with the image hosts of the organization; the OpenAPI description marks such a string with x-safe-html (written once in bb-api-words), the generated types say SafeHtml for it and the client makes the value (SEC-RICHTEXT). The editor's preview reads the hosts from GET /content/image-hosts; the content security policy of a document lists them in img-src (read at most every 10 seconds).
  • The browser side is a controller. web/app/src/shared/editing/long-text.ts holds the lock on the first key, the heartbeat, the two drafts (browser-drafts.ts: one storage key, by person and by what the draft is for, 30 days) and the three save states; useLongText puts it on a screen, useVersionWatch does the check every 30 seconds and on return to the tab.

Amendment (M3 WP-06 fix round)

  • A change never carries long text. PATCH /issues/{issue} takes no description; a body that names it is refused. ARCH-VERSIONED refuses any change of a record (a body with version) that holds a long-text property (LONG_TEXT_PROPERTIES in bb-api-words) unless the route is marked x-long-text. Making a new record has no version and no lock, so it may take the text.
  • Who is editing is asked when the box opens. GET /edit-locks?kind&id&part says who holds the lock, without taking it (the same rules as taking it); the box shows Ana is editing before the first key and opens when the holder lets go.
  • Drafts in the browser belong to a person who is known and are gone after Sign out. None is read or written before the page knows who is signed in; a sign-out on purpose forgets them all, a session that is lost keeps them.

Amendment (M3 WP-10)

  • A refused save for a changed text lets go of the lock. When a save finds that the text changed since (edit.version_changed) the page stops the heartbeat, so it also releases the lock; otherwise others would read that the person is editing until the lease ran out. A lock that ran out or was taken over is not the person's any more and is left alone. The load run found it: locks were still held when it ended.
  • Show changes marks the words and names who (M3-F54): the comparison underlines and fills the words the other text does not have, and the note that the text changed after the person started says who changed it, from the history and the way the reader may see people.
  • The scenarios of ten people are in web/app/e2e/concurrent/ (ten Playwright contexts) and in cargo xtask load --people 10 (the API at speed, both databases, two minutes in cargo xtask ci, --nightly for thirty); the invariants after a run are listed in architecture §11. A lock must also end by itself within the lease for an editor who vanished: no lock row ends later than the lease from now, nobody holds a lock once the leases are over, and the draft of the vanished editor is still there. These rules are written once, in bb-load-check. Enforced by TEST-CONCURRENT and, for the browser part of the locks, TEST-EDIT-LOCKS.
  • A lock covers only the long text. A change of another field of the record (a status, a change of many issues) since the person started is no conflict for the save of the text: Ctx::version_for_text writes the text on the version the record has now when no event after the sent version changed this text. The write still compares that version, so a change that lands in between is refused (ARCH-VERSIONED). A change of the text itself still gives edit.version_changed and Compare and save. Found by the scenario of ten people: the save compared the version of the whole issue.

ADR-0020: Architecture is checked by many small checks, and the checks are checked

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

AI agents implement Bugaboo. Written rules drift unless machines enforce them. One big "lint everything" step is slow, hard to understand and tempting to skip.

Decision

  • One catalogue (tools/checks/catalog.toml) lists every check: ID, plain-language title, the rule it enforces, the tool, when it runs (edit · commit · push · CI · nightly · release) and which files trigger it. cargo xtask implements them; lefthook, Claude Code hooks and CI only call xtask.
  • Many small checks instead of one big one: each enforces one rule, runs only when its files change, and explains itself in one sentence with a link to the rule.
  • Checks for the checks (META):
    • every catalogue entry is implemented, and nothing is implemented without an entry;
    • every check has a failing and a passing example;
    • every file type in the repository is covered by a formatter or linter, so a new kind of file forces a new check;
    • a new crate, package or folder needs a module-map entry first;
    • every "must" rule in the docs names its check or says "review" with a reason (META-RULE-TRACE);
    • all three callers use the same lists;
    • suppressions need a reason and an issue ID, and may not quietly grow (META-SUPPRESS);
    • edit- and commit-time checks stay fast.
  • Agents get edit-time checks after every file change, so mistakes are fixed while the context is fresh.

Consequences

  • Adding a rule means: write it in the docs, add a catalogue entry, implement it in xtask, and add the two examples. The meta checks fail until all four are done.
  • The architecture documentation stays true, because drift breaks the build.

Alternatives considered

  • Review only: doesn't scale with agents. Rejected.
  • Separate hook scripts per tool: differ between Windows and Linux and drift from CI. Rejected.

Enforced by

META-CATALOG, META-FIXTURES, META-COVERAGE, META-NEW-MODULE, META-RULE-TRACE, META-WIRING, META-SUPPRESS, META-SPEED (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0021: Issue IDs, counting or random

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

Counting IDs (WEB-142) are easy to say aloud, but they reveal how many issues a project has and how fast it grows. Anyone who sees two IDs a week apart can estimate activity. That can be sensitive business information, and for small teams it can say something about individual people.

Decision

  • Every issue keeps its internal UUIDv7. The readable ID is the project's short name plus a code chosen per project:
    • Counting: WEB-142.
    • Random: WEB-K7Q2X — 5 characters (configurable 4–8) from Crockford's Base32 alphabet (no I, L, O, U, so no look-alike letters), drawn from a secure random source; on a collision, draw again.
  • The organization default starts as random (security first); each project can choose.
  • Changing the mode or moving an issue to another project gives it a new readable ID; the old ID keeps redirecting (issue_alias table), so links never break.
  • Search, links in text (WEB-K7Q2X becomes a chip) and the API accept both kinds.
  • No other public identifier counts up either: API resources use readable IDs or UUIDs, removed people get random labels, and no screen shows totals that include hidden items.

Consequences

  • The issue chip parser (bb-markdown) recognizes SHORT-CODE for both forms.
  • People in random-ID projects can't guess neighboring issues, which also makes probing for hidden issues harder.

Alternatives considered

  • Counting only: leaks volume. Rejected as the only option.
  • UUIDs in the UI: too long to read or say. Rejected.

Enforced by

TEST-ISSUE-IDS, ARCH-NO-COUNTERS (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

Amendment (M3, 2026-10-09)

  • Moving an issue to another project gives it an ID of the new project (in that project's mode) and keeps the old ID in issue_alias, like a change of mode. M3 moves an issue only into a project that has its issue type and own fields; the preview names the issues it skips and why (decision M3-Q4). Enforced by: TEST-ISSUE-IDS.

Amendment (M3, WP-03)

  • The mode is the setting issues.id-mode (Random IDs or Counting IDs, project level and organization level, changed by the project's lead). A sub-project follows its parent until it chooses, like every setting in layers (ADR-0018). The length of a random code is the setting issues.id-length (4 to 8 symbols, 5 to start, organization level); when the short codes of a project run out, the code gets one symbol longer by itself.
  • Changing the mode of a project (setting or resetting it) gives every issue of the project, and of the sub-projects that follow it, also the issues in the trash, a code of the new mode in the same change, writes one event for each renewed issue (its ID changed from the old to the new one, by the person who changed the mode), and keeps each old code in issue_alias with its project. A key is found by the short name of the project (now or an old one) and the code (now or an old one); the answer holds the current ID. A code that was given out is never given out again in its project, not even to another issue: the stored counter only goes up, and a counting number or a random draw also skips every code and alias that is taken. A random code always holds at least one letter, so it can never be read as a counting number.
  • When the organization's default changes (2026-10-10): projects that follow the organization default give their new issues the new mode. Their existing issues keep their IDs, and nothing is renewed. IDs made before and after the change both work (nothing is renewed there). Only a change of the mode of a project itself (setting or resetting it) renews the IDs of its issues (M3-F20).
  • The counting number is the one counter of the product (issue_counter, one row per project, raised inside the change that makes the issue, so two writers wait for each other and no number is skipped). ARCH-NO-COUNTERS names the files that may use it. Random codes come from the secure random source; a clash with a code of the project is drawn again.
  • Enforced by: TEST-ISSUE-IDS (the tests of these rules exist by name and the database ones run on both databases), ARCH-NO-COUNTERS.

Amendment (M1)

  • Records keep a UUIDv7 (time-ordered). A person's ID is a fully random UUIDv4 instead, so it does not show when the account was made.
  • bb-core does no I/O and builds for WebAssembly, so it never reads the clock or the system's random source. An ID is made from a time and random bytes that the caller passes in (from_parts, IdSource); the server's context supplies the real ones (WP-05).
  • Checked by ARCH-WASM (bb-core builds for wasm32-unknown-unknown) and the tests person_ids_are_random_version_4 and from_parts_puts_the_time_into_the_id in crates/bb-core/src/id.rs.

Amendment (M3 WP-08)

  • Renewal is a job after the first step (M3-F27). Changing the mode of a project with at most 1,000 issues (BULK_JOB_ABOVE) renews all of them inside the change, as before. A bigger project renews the first 100 issues (BULK_STEP) inside the change and queues the job issues.renew-ids, which renews 100 more in each step, one change per step, until none is left. The payload names the project and the person who changed the mode, whose name stays on the event of each renewed ID. Issues made meanwhile already get codes of the new mode; a project whose mode changes again meanwhile is renewed to the mode it has now. Each step is idempotent (it renews only issues whose code is not of the mode).
  • Moving an issue into another project (ISS-09, WP-08) gives it a code of the new project's mode and short name in the same change, keeps the old key in issue_alias, and writes a second event (the key changed) next to the event of the project change, so the history names both.

ADR-0022: Who sees people is part of the permission model

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04 · refined by ADR-0025

Context

Names of people appear in many places: reported by, assigned to, last changed by, comment and history authors, followers, "… is editing", time entries, mentions, avatars, e-mails, exports, the assistant. Under GDPR, organizations may need to hide who did what from some roles (for example external guests, or works-council agreements).

Decision

  • Who sees people is configured per role on the project tree, like field permissions, for each kind of people information: Names, Role only ("a Team member") or Hidden ("Someone").
  • Every place that shows a person uses one type, PersonRef, which is resolved for the viewer by bb-policy into a name, a role label or Someone. Raw person data never reaches serialization directly.
  • If a viewer can't see names for a kind of information, they also can't search, sort, group or filter by it; the field behaves like a hidden field (SEC-06).
  • Edit-lock notices follow the same rule: "Someone is editing the description".
  • Mentions: people who can't see names can only mention groups or roles.

Consequences

  • One resolution point; history, notifications, exports, MCP and the assistant automatically obey it.
  • A tiny cost per rendered person (cached per request).

Alternatives considered

  • Treat each people field as an ordinary field only: misses comment authors, history, presence and avatars. Rejected.

Enforced by

ARCH-PERSON-REF, SEC-MATRIX (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0023: Development ports and test setup

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

The main development PC runs several other Vite projects (ports 5173 and 5200–5319 are taken). Default ports would clash, and Vite silently moving to another port hides the problem and breaks Playwright's server checks.

Decision

  • Vite builds the browser app and runs the dev server; Vitest runs unit tests for browser code; Playwright runs end-to-end and concurrency tests.
  • All local ports come from tools/dev/ports.json (single source), in the range 47200–48099 (see the amendment below), which is free on the main PC and outside Windows' dynamic port range.
  • Every tool uses strictPort: true (or the equivalent) and fails with a clear message naming tools/dev/ports.json if a port is busy.
  • Playwright starts its own server instance (e2eServer, and one per worker from e2eWorkersFrom) with a fresh copy of the sample organization (architecture §11), so tests never touch a developer's data.
  • No tool may use a framework's default port (5173, 4173, 3000, 8080, 51204).

Consequences

  • Several Bugaboo checkouts on one machine use different blocks of the range (amendment below), so they can build and test at the same time.

Amendment (M2 WP-04): a block of ports for each work folder

Builders in different work folders (ADR-0024) ran their end-to-end tests and their throwaway PostgreSQL at the same time on the same ports, and one run answered for another. Each work folder now has its own block:

  • A block is 100 ports. bugaboo.winN uses block N, which starts at first + (N − 1) · stride = 47200 + (N − 1) · 100: win1 47200–47299, win2 47300–47399, … win9 48000–48099. Nothing in 47200–48099 is reserved on the main PC, and the dynamic range starts at 49152.
  • Any other folder (CI, a fresh clone, the master) uses block 1. The variable BUGABOO_PORT_BLOCK names another block (1 to 9) and wins over the name of the folder. A work folder with a number outside 1 to 9, or a variable outside it, is an error that names the variable.
  • tools/dev/ports.json stays the single source: it holds first, stride, blocks and the offset of each port inside a block (server 0, web 1, … postgres 40). BB_PORTS_FILE is gone.
  • One reader per language: web/tooling/ports.ts (Vite, Vitest, Playwright, the end-to-end workers) and xtask/src/dev.rs (cargo xtask dev, db, ci). Both derive the block from the name of the repository folder. Nothing else names a port; the tests that write a port as a text in a fake address never listen on it.
  • Every tool still uses strictPort: a busy port fails and names tools/dev/ports.json.

Enforced by: DEV-PORTS (the layout of the file: the range, the offsets, no duplicates), the tests dev_ports_* in xtask/src/dev.rs and dist_01_every_work_folder_has_a_block_of_its_own in web/tooling/ports.test.ts.

Alternatives considered

  • Random free ports: avoids clashes but makes URLs unpredictable for people and documentation. Rejected.

Enforced by

DEV-PORTS, TEST-SAMPLE-DATA, TEST-CONCURRENT (see tools/checks/catalog.toml).

ADR-0024: Master repository in a synced folder, work folders outside it

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-04

Context

The repository lives in OneDrive. Build output (Rust target, node_modules, caches, test reports) would make OneDrive sync gigabytes and lock files during builds. GitHub comes later; until then the repository is local. The developer already uses a pattern for this: a master repository plus clones in <work root>\<project>.winN, each on its own branch WINn.

Decision

  • Master: <master> holds main and the shared history. Nothing is built or installed there; it only receives pushes and fast-forward merges.
  • Work folders (outside OneDrive), clones of the master with origin pointing to it:
    • <work root>\bugaboo.win1, branch WIN1: the lead's folder. Work packages are merged here, cargo xtask ci runs here, and only then is main fast-forwarded.
    • bugaboo.win2, bugaboo.win3, …, branches WIN2, WIN3, …: one per builder agent working in parallel. Each starts from main, pushes its branch when its work package is done, and is reset to main for the next one.
  • Integration: in win1: fetch WINn, merge, run cargo xtask ci; push WIN1; in the master: git merge --ff-only WIN1. main therefore only ever moves to states that passed CI.
  • Build folders stay inside each work folder (they are outside OneDrive already). Machine-specific overrides go into .cargo/config.local.toml, which the committed .cargo/config.toml includes optionally (works on stable Cargo) and Git ignores.
  • Guard: cargo xtask refuses to build, test or install anything when it runs inside a synced folder, with a message pointing to the work folders.
  • Later: when the repository moves to GitHub, GitHub becomes origin for the work folders and the master becomes one more clone; nothing else changes.

Consequences

  • OneDrive only syncs source files and Git objects, not build output.
  • Parallel builders never share a build folder, so they don't block each other.
  • Each work folder needs its own build (several GB each); plan the disk space for it.

Alternatives considered

  • One shared CARGO_TARGET_DIR for the user: would also change the developer's other Rust projects on the same machine. Rejected.
  • Git worktrees of the master: Git state would live inside the synced folder and be written by every agent at once. Clones keep each folder independent. Rejected.

Amendment (M1, 2026-10-05)

  • Edit hook decides by the edited file. The Claude Code session often runs in the master, so $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR points into OneDrive for every agent. The PostToolUse command therefore looks at the edited file: it finds the nearest folder above it with .git and xtask/Cargo.toml, skips files in the synced folder or outside any work folder, and runs that work folder's own cargo xtask hook post-edit. Enforced by META-WIRING (the command is compared byte for byte).
  • Agent memory in the repository. Claude Code's memory files live in .claude/memory/ and are committed like any doc; the master's ignored .claude/settings.local.json sets autoMemoryDirectory to bugaboo.win1/.claude/memory, so a session started in the master reads and writes the work folder's copy (never files in OneDrive).
  • Builds refused in the master by Cargo itself. Besides the xtask guard, the master's ignored .cargo/config.local.toml sets build.rustc-wrapper to tools/dev/refuse-build.cmd, which exits with a message, so even a plain cargo build or an editor's Rust tooling started in the synced folder stops before anything is built. Tool data that does not belong in the synced folder (for example CodeGraph's index database) lives in a work folder, not in the master. Checked by review (the lead's set-up check).
  • Git hooks in every work folder. cargo xtask setup installs lefthook and the hooks; the master gets none, because nothing is committed there.
  • If OneDrive turns the master's folders into cloud placeholders, git merge --ff-only WIN1 fails with "unable to unlink", "cannot create directory" or "Directory not empty", and fsutil reparsepoint query <folder> shows a tag instead of error 4390. Recovery, with nothing open in the master: move every top-level entry except .git into a backup folder outside the synced folder, run git checkout HEAD -- . in the master, then repeat the fast-forward. No reset --hard, no copying files by hand. Checked by review (the lead runs the fsutil query when a fast-forward fails).

Amendment (M3 WP-10)

  • The browsers of the end-to-end tests. cargo xtask setup also runs the pinned Playwright's install for Chromium and WebKit (the phone project in WebKit, M2-F12). Which revision of each browser is installed is decided by the Playwright version in package-lock.json, so the versions are pinned like the other tools. Playwright keeps the browsers in one cache of the user (ms-playwright), shared by all work folders, and skips what is there; they are the one thing setup does not put into .tools/, because each copy is several hundred megabytes.

Enforced by

BUILD-LOCATION and META-WIRING (see tools/checks/catalog.toml); the recovery steps by review.

ADR-0025: Roles, groups and assignments on the project tree

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-05 · refines ADR-0004 and ADR-0022

Context

ADR-0004 says that one policy engine (bb-policy) makes every decision and that data leaves the domain only as Authorized<T>. ADR-0022 says that people are shown through PersonRef by the rules of Who sees people. Neither says what exactly a role holds, where a role counts, what wins when two rules disagree, or how the M1 administrator flag turns into roles. M2 builds all of it (SEC-01, SEC-02, SEC-03, SEC-04, SEC-06, SEC-08, AUTH-07, PRIV-12, PRIV-13), and the open questions M2-Q1 … M2-Q7 were answered by accepting every proposal. This record writes the model down so that WP-05 can build it without asking; the details a builder needs (the tables, the shapes of answers) are in architecture §7, Authorization model.

Decision

1. One permission catalogue
  • One Rust enum, Permission, in bb-policy, is the only list of permissions (coding standards §1). Every permission has a key (see-projects), a topic (Projects, People, Settings; later milestones add Issues, Documents, Time), a plain sentence as a message key (permission.see-projects: "See the project and what is in it"), where it counts and a kind for access keys. The API description, the role page, SEC-MATRIX and the docs are made from the enum. Enforced by: ARCH-PERMS (every route declares one catalogue key or public, signed-in, own-account, by-record; every permission is used and has its message), SEC-MATRIX.
  • Where it counts: an organization permission (make top-level projects, people, invitations, groups, roles, organization settings, the status page) counts only from a role given for the whole organization; a project permission counts in projects. A role given on a project that holds an organization permission gives nothing for it, and the role page says so.
  • Kinds (for access keys, decision 8): See (changes nothing), Change (work in projects), Manage (people, roles, settings).
  • The M2 catalogue has 14 permissions (the table is in architecture §7). A later milestone adds its permissions to the enum with their sentences, kinds and starting values in the same change (issues M3, documents M11, time M6); a permission no route uses fails ARCH-PERMS.
2. Assignments: who has which role, and where it counts
  • An assignment is one row of Who has which role: a person or a group, a role or No access, and where it counts: Whole organization, Only this project, or This project and its sub-projects (SEC-02).
  • Whole organization rows exist only in Organization settings; project rows only on a project. No access is set only on a project and always covers This project and its sub-projects (M2-Q1).
  • A person or group may hold several roles on one project, but never a role and No access on the same project: such a change is refused with a sentence that says which row is in the way.
  • Groups are flat in M2 (nested groups are L). A person's groups are read once per request with their assignments.
3. Evaluation order and No access

For an actor and a place (the organization, or a project with its parents), bb-policy decides without I/O, from one port call that loads the actor's assignments for the place and its parents:

  1. Nobody signed in: only public routes. Signed in without an applicable assignment: nothing (default deny, SEC-01).
  2. Applicable are the actor's own and their groups' assignments for the whole organization, those on a parent of the project with This project and its sub-projects, and those on the project itself.
  3. Each applicable row has a rank: first the depth of its project (whole organization lowest), then the person's own row above a row of one of their groups.
  4. No access (M2-Q1): the highest-ranked No access row removes every role row of equal or lower rank. So it wins over roles given higher up, over a role of one of the person's groups on the same project, and over another group's role on the same project. A role given lower down (on a sub-project below the No access), or given to the person directly on the same project where a group has No access, still counts: the nearer, more personal row decides.
  5. The permissions are the union of the remaining roles, filtered by where it counts; then an access key narrows them (decision 8).
  6. The field mask and the Who sees people levels are worked out from the same remaining roles (decisions 10 and 11).

Evaluations are cached for one request and never across requests, so a role taken away counts from the next request. Enforced by: review (the cache is a field of the request context, which a reviewer sees in the diff), backed by the tests sec_03_no_access_on_a_sub_project_wins_over_a_role_from_above, sec_03_a_role_taken_away_counts_from_the_next_request and the property tests of WP-05 (a new role never takes a permission away; No access never adds one), and SEC-MATRIX.

4. Starting roles are editable copies
  • One Rust definition in bb-policy holds the six starting roles of SEC-08 and M2-Q5 (Administrator, Project lead, Team member, Contributor, Viewer, Guest): their permissions, field levels, Who sees people levels and order (architecture §7). A system use case makes editable copies from it once, at the first start, with events and security-log entries (never in a migration). After that the definition is read only by Reset to the starting permissions, which a copy keeps through a starting mark that renaming does not remove.
  • A starting role can be renamed, changed and deleted like any other role; the last-administrator rule (decision 6) still holds. Enforced by: the tests sec_08_starting_roles_are_made_once_and_can_be_changed_and_reset and sec_08_a_changed_starting_role_can_be_reset.
  • The order of roles (the starting order, then new roles where an administrator puts them) decides the label of a person shown as Role only when they hold several roles: the first in the order.
5. The administrator flag becomes the Administrator role
  • Migration m0003 keeps the list of M1 administrators. In the same change that makes the starting roles at the first start, each of them gets the Administrator role for the whole organization, with its event and security-log entry; afterwards the flag no longer exists in the database, the API (/auth/me answers the person's organization permissions instead) or the browser app. Enforced by: the test sec_08_m1_administrators_become_administrators_and_nobody_else_does (both databases).
  • Setup (AUTH-09) stays open while nobody can manage roles for the whole organization (decision 6 makes that the state of a fresh installation only). Making the first administrator makes the starting roles if they do not exist yet and gives the person the Administrator role for the whole organization, in one change.
6. Nobody locks the organization out, and nobody gives what they do not have
  • The last administrator: a change that would leave no person who holds both Manage roles and Decide who has which role for the whole organization (through their own row or a group) is refused, with a sentence that says why. This covers removing a row, taking a person out of a group, deleting a group or role, and taking a permission out of a role. Enforced by: the test sec_08_nobody_can_remove_the_last_way_to_manage_roles.
  • No access never locks out the people above: Decide who has which role on a project is kept for a person who holds it through a row that the project's No access removed, only when that row is strictly above the No access (a parent project, or the whole organization). A row at the depth of a No access that removes it, such as a role of the person's group next to their own No access on the same project, is removed as a whole: otherwise a person could lift their own No access. They see the project's name and short name in Who has which role and can take the No access away again; they see nothing in the project. Enforced by: the tests sec_03_no_access_cannot_lock_out_the_people_who_decide_roles_above and sec_03_decide_roles_is_kept_only_from_rows_strictly_above_the_no_access (engine), and sec_03_decide_roles_is_not_kept_from_a_row_at_the_same_depth_as_the_no_access (both databases).
  • No escalation: a person can add a permission to a role, or give a role, only when they hold every permission of it at that place themselves (organization permissions are left out of this comparison for a role given on a project, because they count nowhere there). A role given with its sub-projects reaches the sub-projects made later as well as those that exist, so the giver holds it through rows that reach sub-projects themselves (their rows for the project alone do not count) and in every sub-project that exists (a lead for one project only cannot make themselves lead of everything below it, now or when a sub-project is made). Putting a person into a group gives them every role of the group, so the same holds for each row of the group. The check runs inside the change, after the policy lock (making a project takes the lock too), so two changes cannot both pass on what was stored before; the same holds for adding to a role and for resetting one, which read the role and what the person holds there. A level is held to the same rule: taking a project's setting away is setting the level that then applies there (the nearest parent's, else the role's own). Enforced by: the tests sec_08_nobody_adds_a_permission_they_do_not_hold_to_a_role, sec_02_nobody_gives_a_role_with_more_than_they_hold_there, sec_02_nobody_gives_a_role_with_sub_projects_they_do_not_hold_there, sec_02_a_role_with_sub_projects_needs_a_row_that_reaches_sub_projects, sec_02_a_group_with_a_role_for_sub_projects_is_not_joined_by_a_lead_of_one_project and sec_04_nobody_raises_a_level_by_taking_an_override_away.
  • Manage groups does not lift a No access: taking a person out of a group, or deleting a group, that has No access rows takes those rows away for them, so it needs Decide who has which role at each project where the group has one, like taking the row away itself. Giving, adding to a group, taking out of a group and deleting a group are the four ways a person's rights change through a group. Enforced by: the test sec_02_manage_groups_does_not_lift_a_no_access_of_the_group.
7. Two-step sign-in is a switch on the role
  • A role has a switch Two-step sign-in for everyone with this role (AUTH-03, M1-F45), stored with the role; the text setting security.two-step-required-roles is removed with its stored values (WP-05). security.two-step-required stays: it asks it of everybody.
  • A person needs a second step when the organization switch is on or any role they hold anywhere (own row or group, any place) has the switch on. It takes effect at the next request: until the person has a code app or a passkey, their session can only set one up. Enforced by: the test auth_03_a_role_that_requires_two_step_sign_in_makes_its_people_set_it_up_first (WP-09).
  • Access keys follow it (M2-F46): while a person is asked for a second step, the keys they made are refused too, with 403 auth.second_step_required and an entry in the security log, and work again as soon as they have set one up. Without this, an old key of a person who is asked for a second step would still work and could even switch the requirement off for its owner. Enforced by: the tests auth_03_a_key_made_before_the_switch_is_refused_until_its_owner_sets_up_a_second_step and auth_03_a_key_cannot_switch_off_the_requirement_of_its_owner (WP-09).
8. Access keys can only narrow
  • What it may do (M2-Q6) is one of three choices: See only (permissions of kind See, every field at most Can see), See and change (See and Change), Everything I can do (all kinds); under More options, single permissions instead. Optionally a list of projects: the key then counts only in them and their sub-projects (by project ID, so a move does not change it) and gives nothing for the whole organization.
  • At every use the key's permissions are the owner's evaluation at that place intersected with the key's choice and projects; a key never widens anything, and follows its owner's roles at once (AUTH-07). No key reaches the owner's own sign-in data (password, passkeys, two-step, sessions, access keys), and a key is refused while its owner is asked for a second step (decision 7).
  • What no key holds (decision): whatever its choice, even Everything I can do and single permissions, a key never keeps Invite people, Manage people, Manage groups, Manage roles, Decide who has which role, Decide what roles see and Change organization settings (lead decision of 2026-10-06, so that a key cannot switch off the two-step requirement, open signing up or change how long sessions last). They stay in the app, where the person is signed in, so a stolen key cannot invite an administrator, take roles away or change the settings of the organization. The list is defined once beside the kinds, in bb-policy (NOT_FOR_KEYS); narrowing removes them, the key form does not offer them and the server refuses a key made with one. Enforced by: the tests auth_07_a_key_never_invites_people_or_changes_roles_whatever_its_choice (it also tries the settings of the organization), auth_07_single_permissions_of_a_key_never_include_those_a_key_never_holds and the property test auth_07_a_key_can_do_only_what_its_owner_can_and_its_scopes_allow (WP-09).
  • Keys end with Sign out everywhere (decision): the person's keys are deleted in the same change, each one with an entry in the security log. A password change ends the other sessions and leaves the keys. Enforced by: the test auth_07_sign_out_everywhere_ends_the_keys_and_a_password_change_leaves_them (WP-09).
  • Every key runs out: 90 days unless the person picks another date, never later than the organization's longest time (an organization setting, default and most 365 days). The settings are declared in the registry by WP-09. Enforced by: the tests auth_07_a_key_can_do_only_what_its_owner_can_and_its_scopes_allow (property test), auth_07_a_key_follows_its_owner_losing_a_role_at_once and auth_07_a_key_cannot_change_the_owners_sign_in_data, and SEC-MATRIX (an access key with See only, and one for another project).
9. Every permission change is in the security log

Every change of roles (permissions, two-step switch, name, reset), groups (made, renamed, deleted, members), assignments (including No access), field levels, Who sees people levels, project moves and short names, and access keys (made, deleted, refused) writes its domain event and a security-log entry in the same change (SEC-15). Enforced by: ARCH-EVENTS, and the generated test sec_15_every_change_of_permissions_is_in_the_security_log that runs every management use case (WP-05).

10. Field masks
  • The field catalogue (built-in fields of M2-Q7) is declared once in bb-core; own fields join in M3 (CF-06). Each field has a level per role: Hidden < Can see < Can change. The organization level is the role's own level; a project can set another level for a role, which its sub-projects inherit until one of them sets its own.
  • The mask is the highest level of the remaining roles (decision 3), capped at Can see for a See only key. Authorized<T> carries it and leaves hidden fields out when it is serialized; a hidden field and an unknown one are refused alike. Enforced by: ARCH-AUTHZ-ONLY, ARCH-API-OUT, SEC-MATRIX, and the test sec_06_a_hidden_field_is_not_in_the_answer_and_asking_for_it_fails_like_an_unknown_field.
11. People: PersonRef and the kinds of people information
  • Who sees people (ADR-0022) is set per role and per kind of people information; M2 adds the kind Project members (M2-Q3): member lists of a project. Levels are inherited like field levels; the viewer's level is the most open of their remaining roles (Names > Role only > Hidden).
  • People who manage see names (M2-Q3): in Organization settings, Who has which role and Check access, a viewer who holds Manage people, Manage groups, Manage roles or Decide who has which role at that place always sees names; everybody else sees the people there by the kind Project members. E-mail addresses are part of no PersonRef: only Manage people and the person themselves see them.
  • PersonRef resolves for the viewer, the kind and the place into a name, a role label, Someone, or a random Former user label (PRIV-13); the viewer always sees their own name. A role label and Someone carry no ID of the person. Enforced by: ARCH-PERSON-REF, SEC-MATRIX (people rows), and the tests priv_12_people_are_shown_by_name_role_or_someone_as_the_rules_say and priv_13_former_user_labels_are_random_and_unique.
12. Check access answers with reasons

Check access is a query use case: for a person and a place it lists every permission that counts there with yes or no, every field with its level and every kind of people information with its level, each with its reasons as data (the row, the person or group, the role, the project it is on, whether it is inherited, a No access that decided, or that no role gives it). The browser turns the reasons into sentences from message keys. A reason never names a project the checker cannot see: it says the row is on a project you can't see. Enforced by: the property test sec_03_check_access_explains_every_result_with_the_chain_of_reasons (the decision equals the engine's and the reasons lead to it) and sec_03_check_access_names_no_project_the_checker_cannot_see.

13. Projects and short names
  • A short name (M2-Q4) is 2 to 10 capital letters or digits and starts with a letter (WEB, APP2); it is unique in the organization, old short names included, and can be changed. An old short name stays with its project, so its addresses keep working (project_alias, like issue_alias in ADR-0021); only that project can take it back. One definition, ShortName in bb-core. Enforced by: the tests prj_01_a_short_name_breaks_no_rule_of_m2_q4 and prj_01_an_old_short_name_redirects.
  • Hidden projects stay hidden: a project the person cannot see answers resource.not_found like a missing one, by address and by short name; a visible sub-project of a hidden project is shown at the top and never names its parent. A short name that is taken is told only to people who may make projects at that place, with the same sentence whether the project is hidden or not. Enforced by: SEC-MATRIX, the tests prj_01_a_hidden_project_answers_not_found_like_a_missing_one, prj_01_a_visible_sub_project_of_a_hidden_project_does_not_name_it and prj_01_a_taken_short_name_is_told_only_to_people_who_may_make_projects.
14. Who may change a setting

The registry's changed_by (ADR-0018) maps to the catalogue: Administrators → Change organization settings; Project leads → Change project settings on that project; Each person → only their own value. Enforced by: ARCH-SETTINGS, and the test cfg_06_only_administrators_change_organization_values_and_each_person_only_their_own (WP-07).

Consequences

  • WP-05 builds the engine from this record and architecture §7; WP-08, WP-09, WP-11 and WP-12 put screens and routes on it; SEC-MATRIX (WP-10) runs every route for every starting role, a role on a parent and on a sibling project, No access and two access keys.
  • The deny rule has one exception (decision 6), so administrators cannot be shut out of a sub-project for good; the people above see that the project exists, but not what is in it.
  • Group membership and role assignments are personal data of a new category, organization (where a person works); access keys and the person's own settings are personal data too. The marks are listed in 12-security.md and come from the code into the generated personal-data page when WP-05, WP-07, WP-08 and WP-09 add the entities. Enforced by: DATA-MARKS.
  • Check access tells a checker that a role comes from a project you can't see, so a hidden parent's existence (never its name) shows there.
  • Removing the M1 flag touches every place that read administrator, in Rust and in the browser app (WP-05).

Alternatives considered

  • No access that wins in its whole subtree, even over roles given lower down: simpler, but an organization could then not hide a big project from a group except for one sub-project. Rejected; the nearer row decides, as for field levels.
  • No access only for the people it names, never over a group's role at the same project: a person could not be taken out of one project without leaving their group. Rejected (M2-Q1).
  • Hard-coded roles: SEC-08 asks for editable copies. Rejected.
  • Reading the starting definition at every evaluation (roles as overrides of the definition): a change of the definition in an update would silently change every organization's roles. Rejected; copies are made once.
  • Access keys with their own role: keys could then hold more than their owner. Rejected (AUTH-07: keys only narrow).
  • The deny as a role (No access is a role with no permissions): a role adds, it cannot take away. Rejected.

Enforced by

ARCH-PERMS, ARCH-AUTHZ-ONLY, ARCH-API-OUT, ARCH-PERSON-REF, ARCH-NO-COUNTERS, ARCH-EVENTS, ARCH-SETTINGS, DATA-MARKS and SEC-MATRIX (see tools/checks/catalog.toml), backed by the named tests of WP-05, WP-08, WP-09, WP-11 and WP-12; the per-request cache by review.

ADR-0026: One theme file for everything about how the app looks

Status: Accepted · 2026-10-08 · replaces the styling part of ADR-0010

Context

Requirement (M2C): all UI theming lives in one theming file, the way the sister project the sister project keeps its complete look in defaults/theme.kdl. ADR-0010 made design/tokens.json the source of colors, fonts, sizes, radii and shadows, but let every component keep its own CSS Module. The audit of M2C (section D) found what that costs:

  • 55 CSS modules with 3,261 lines; values that have no token (font-weight: 700 57 times, line heights 38 times, about 50 1px solid borders, a z-index chosen per file, opacities, keyframes);
  • the same rule copied into many modules (the focus ring 22 times, the muted text, .stack, .row), the skip link twice, and forced-colors handling in ten components;
  • the theme list written in tokens.json and again in the settings registry in Rust, held together by a test (M2C-F64);
  • theme names and the data-look attribute written by hand in TypeScript and in the browser tests.

the sister project compiles its theme to CSS in the browser and injects it as a style element. Bugaboo cannot do that: the content security policy is style-src 'self' (SEC-11), so nothing may put a style on the page at run time.

Decision

  1. One file, design/theme.kdl (KDL, like the sister project; decision M2C-Q1). It holds everything: the themes, the choices that change token values, every token with its variants per mode, the contrast rules, the mixins, the keyframes and the rules of every component. Comments are allowed, and each token is one line. It replaces design/tokens.json. Only cargo xtask gen theme reads it (with the kdl crate, pinned like the sister project's); the server and the browser never parse KDL.

  2. Values are tokens, with their variants per mode on the line of the token. A token has a kind (color, font, size, number, duration, easing, shadow, weight, line-height, border-width, layer, opacity) and, besides its value:

    • <theme>= for each of the four themes (colors and shadows), with kind="light" or "dark" on the theme;
    • <theme>-more= for a device that asks for more contrast (prefers-contrast: more);
    • forced= while forced colors are on (forced-colors: active);
    • <choice>= while a choice of the person is on: compact spacing, larger-text, less-motion (which the device can switch on too).

    Every token of ADR-0010 keeps its value; the file adds font weight, line height, border width, layers (z-index), opacity, easing, the brightness of a pressed primary button, and forced colors as a mode. The focus ring is two tokens (ring-width, ring-offset) and one mixin (ring) that every rule uses.

  3. Rules are part rules that use tokens only. part "button[variant=primary]:hover" { background "$accent" } styles every element that says data-part="button" and data-variant="primary". A value is a word, 0, a percentage, or $token (written var(--token) in the output); a length, color, duration, weight, line height, layer or opacity written out is a finding of LINT-CSS and STY-TOKENS. base rules style the page frame (html, body); mixin, keyframes and forced { … }, more-contrast { … }, media "…" { … } blocks complete the language.

  4. Components carry no style values and no class names. They emit data-part, data-state and data-variant, through partOf(part.button, { variants: […], states: […] }) of @bugaboo/ui. The names of the parts and the words a part may have (partWords) are generated into tokens.ts from the rules, so a misspelled part or word is a type error. React Aria's own data-* state attributes (data-hovered, data-pressed, data-selected, data-focus-visible, data-entering, …) are allowed and used: a rule names them as button[hovered].

  5. The file is compiled at build time into one static style sheet, web/packages/ui/src/theme.css (committed, with a copy for the design pages at docs/design/theme.css). The content security policy stays style-src 'self'; no style element or attribute is made at run time. This is where Bugaboo differs from the sister project. Neither file is edited by hand: DOC-GENERATED compares them with the output of cargo xtask gen theme.

  6. The list of themes is written once. The four built-in themes (Daylight, Paper, Dusk, Midnight) and the two that start are defined in the file. gen theme writes them to TypeScript (tokens.ts: themeIds, lightThemeIds, darkThemeIds, the defaults) and to Rust (crates/bb-core/src/settings/themes.rs: the choices of the settings Light theme and Dark theme and their defaults, which catalog.rs names).
